title: == vs equals()
short: == compares primitive values or object references; equals() expresses logical equality.
answer: For objects, == checks reference identity. equals() can be overridden for state equality. If equals is overridden, hashCode must follow the contract.
interview: == compares primitive values or object references; equals() expresses logical equality.

title: equals() and hashCode() contract
short: Equal objects must have equal hash codes.
answer: Hash-based collections use hashCode to locate a bucket and equals to confirm the key. Unequal objects may collide.
followups: What breaks if hashCode is omitted?
interview: Equal objects must have equal hash codes.

title: HashMap internal working
short: HashMap uses a key hash to select a bucket and equals() to identify the key.
answer: HashMap spreads the hash, maps it to a bucket and handles collisions. Modern Java can treeify heavily-collided buckets under suitable conditions. Resize redistributes entries.
interview: HashMap uses a key hash to select a bucket and equals() to identify the key.

title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
short: ArrayList gives fast indexed access; LinkedList is node-based.
answer: ArrayList is usually the better default. LinkedList has O(n) indexed access and only helps for specific operations/access patterns.
followups: Which is better for random access?
interview: ArrayList gives fast indexed access; LinkedList is node-based.

title: HashSet vs LinkedHashSet vs TreeSet
short: HashSet has no ordering guarantee, LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order, TreeSet maintains sorted order.
answer: Hash-based sets usually provide expected O(1) basic operations. TreeSet is generally O(log n).
interview: HashSet has no ordering guarantee, LinkedHashSet preserves insertion order, TreeSet maintains sorted order.

title: How to create an immutable class
short: Prevent observable state changes after construction.
answer: Use private final fields, constructor initialization, no setters, defensive copies and final class where appropriate.
code: public final class User { private final String name; public User(String n){name=n;} }
interview: Prevent observable state changes after construction.

title: final vs finally vs finalize
short: final is a keyword, finally is exception cleanup flow, finalize is obsolete for resource management.
answer: final restricts reassignment/overriding/inheritance. finally normally executes after try/catch. Do not rely on finalize for cleanup.
interview: final is a keyword, finally is exception cleanup flow, finalize is obsolete for resource management.

title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions
short: Checked exceptions must be handled/declared; unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException.
answer: Choose based on whether callers can reasonably recover and where errors are translated.
interview: Checked exceptions must be handled/declared; unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException.

title: Try-with-resources
short: It automatically closes AutoCloseable resources.
answer: Resources close even when exceptions occur; close failures can be represented as suppressed exceptions.
interview: It automatically closes AutoCloseable resources.

title: Abstract class vs interface
short: Abstract classes can share state/implementation; interfaces define contracts and support multiple inheritance of type.
answer: Use abstract classes for genuine shared base behavior/state and interfaces for capabilities/contracts.
code:
interface Auditable{void audit();}
abstract class Base{Long id;}
interview: Abstract classes can share state/implementation; interfaces define contracts and support multiple inheritance of type.

title: Default and static interface methods
short: Default methods provide instance behavior; static methods belong to the interface.
answer: Default methods help evolve interfaces. Static interface methods are called through the interface name and are not instance overrides.
code: interface Loggable { default void log(){} static String level(){return "INFO";} }
interview: Default methods provide instance behavior; static methods belong to the interface.

title: Optional usage
short: Optional models an expected possibly-absent return value.
answer: It is particularly useful for return types. It should not automatically replace null in every field or parameter.
interview: Optional models an expected possibly-absent return value.

title: Functional interface
short: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method.
answer: It can be targeted by lambdas/method references. Default and static methods do not count.
interview: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method.

title: Lambda expression
short: A lambda is a concise implementation of a functional interface.
answer: Types are inferred from the target type. Captured local variables must be final or effectively final.
interview: A lambda is a concise implementation of a functional interface.

title: Record
short: A record is a concise data carrier with generated accessors and value methods.
answer: Records are final with final component references, but referenced objects can still be mutable.
interview: A record is a concise data carrier with generated accessors and value methods.

title: Virtual threads
short: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads suited to high-concurrency blocking workloads.
answer: They make thread-per-task models practical at large concurrency. They do not make CPU work intrinsically faster.
interview: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads suited to high-concurrency blocking workloads.

title: synchronized
short: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and memory visibility around a monitor.
answer: Only one thread holds a monitor at a time. Synchronization also establishes happens-before relationships.
interview: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and memory visibility around a monitor.

title: volatile vs AtomicInteger
short: volatile provides visibility; AtomicInteger provides atomic operations too.
answer: volatile does not make count++ atomic. AtomicInteger supports increment and compare-and-set style operations.
interview: volatile provides visibility; AtomicInteger provides atomic operations too.

title: Deadlock and prevention
short: Deadlock is cyclic waiting for locks.
answer: Prevent with consistent lock ordering, small lock scopes, avoiding nested locks and timed acquisition where appropriate.
interview: Deadlock is cyclic waiting for locks.

title: Heap vs stack
short: Objects are generally managed on the heap; each thread has its own call stack.
answer: Heap is shared and GC-managed. A stack holds method frames and local execution state.
interview: Objects are generally managed on the heap; each thread has its own call stack.

title: Garbage collection
short: GC reclaims objects that are no longer reachable.
answer: Collectors trade throughput, latency and memory footprint. Allocation rate and retention still matter.
interview: GC reclaims objects that are no longer reachable.

title: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
short: String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and unsynchronized; StringBuffer is synchronized.
answer: StringBuilder is normally preferred for iterative construction.
interview: String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and unsynchronized; StringBuffer is synchronized.

title: Comparable vs Comparator
short: Comparable defines natural order; Comparator defines external ordering.
answer: Comparator supports multiple contextual sorting strategies.
interview: Comparable defines natural order; Comparator defines external ordering.

title: map vs flatMap
short: map is one-to-one transformation; flatMap transforms and flattens nested streams.
answer: flatMap is useful for one-to-many relationships.
interview: map is one-to-one transformation; flatMap transforms and flattens nested streams.

title: parallelStream
short: parallelStream is concurrent stream processing and is not automatically faster.
answer: It can help sufficiently large CPU-bound independent work and hurt for blocking I/O/shared state/small data.
interview: parallelStream is concurrent stream processing and is not automatically faster.

title: Microservice characteristics
short: Microservices are independently deployable components aligned to business capabilities.
answer: Good boundaries consider business ownership and deployment independence. They add distributed-system complexity.
interview: Microservices are independently deployable components aligned to business capabilities.

title: API Gateway vs Load Balancer
short: A load balancer distributes traffic; a gateway also applies API-level policies.
answer: Gateways commonly handle auth, rate limits, routing and transformation.
interview: A load balancer distributes traffic; a gateway also applies API-level policies.

title: Service discovery
short: It lets clients find healthy service instances without hardcoded addresses.
answer: Discovery can be client/server-side. Kubernetes commonly provides service discovery via DNS/services.
interview: It lets clients find healthy service instances without hardcoded addresses.

title: Sync vs async communication
short: Synchronous calls wait for responses; async messaging decouples timing.
answer: Async improves buffering/decoupling but introduces eventual consistency and duplicate handling.
interview: Synchronous calls wait for responses; async messaging decouples timing.

title: Saga pattern
short: A Saga coordinates local transactions with compensating business actions.
answer: Each service commits locally. Compensation is a new business action, not a distributed DB rollback.
interview: A Saga coordinates local transactions with compensating business actions.

title: Outbox pattern
short: Business state and an event record are committed in one local transaction.
answer: A publisher sends outbox events later. Consumers still need idempotency.
interview: Business state and an event record are committed in one local transaction.

title: Idempotency
short: Repeating a request produces the same intended business result.
answer: Idempotency keys are useful for payments/order creation; persist key and outcome.
interview: Repeating a request produces the same intended business result.

title: Retry policy
short: Retry transient failures with bounded attempts.
answer: Use timeouts, exponential backoff and jitter. Avoid retrying non-idempotent operations without safeguards.
interview: Retry transient failures with bounded attempts.

title: Bulkhead pattern
short: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one dependency cannot consume all capacity.
answer: Separate executors, pools or concurrency limits reduce blast radius.
interview: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one dependency cannot consume all capacity.

title: Eventual consistency
short: Different services may temporarily see different state before convergence.
answer: Define acceptable stale windows and user-visible intermediate states.
interview: Different services may temporarily see different state before convergence.

title: Resilience patterns
short: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and graceful degradation control failures.
answer: Each protects a different failure mode. Combining them requires careful limits to avoid retry storms.
interview: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and graceful degradation control failures.

title: Distributed tracing
short: Tracing follows requests across services using trace/span context.
answer: Trace is end-to-end; spans represent operations. Propagation preserves correlation.
interview: Tracing follows requests across services using trace/span context.

title: Microservice monitoring
short: Use metrics, structured logs, traces and health signals tied to user impact.
answer: Monitor rate, errors, latency, saturation, JVM, DB pools and broker lag.
interview: Use metrics, structured logs, traces and health signals tied to user impact.

title: API versioning
short: Prefer backward-compatible evolution and explicit versions for breaking changes.
answer: Additive changes and deprecation reduce consumer disruption.
interview: Prefer backward-compatible evolution and explicit versions for breaking changes.

title: Rate limiting
short: Rate limiting controls traffic per identity/resource.
answer: Token bucket, leaky bucket and sliding windows are common; distributed systems may need shared state.
interview: Rate limiting controls traffic per identity/resource.

title: Message broker
short: A broker decouples producers and consumers and can buffer work.
answer: Kafka, RabbitMQ and cloud messaging have different ordering/delivery models.
interview: A broker decouples producers and consumers and can buffer work.

title: Kafka topic/partition/group
short: Topics hold records, partitions provide parallelism and per-partition ordering, groups divide consumption.
answer: More consumers than partitions do not increase that group's partition parallelism.
interview: Topics hold records, partitions provide parallelism and per-partition ordering, groups divide consumption.

title: At-least-once vs at-most-once
short: At-least-once can duplicate; at-most-once can lose messages.
answer: Exactly-once must be considered end-to-end. Idempotent processing is often the practical target.
interview: At-least-once can duplicate; at-most-once can lose messages.

title: Service mesh
short: A service mesh moves service-to-service networking policies into infrastructure proxies/nodes.
answer: It can provide mTLS, routing and telemetry but adds platform complexity.
interview: A service mesh moves service-to-service networking policies into infrastructure proxies/nodes.

title: Debug production 500
short: Preserve evidence and correlate the failure through logs, metrics and traces.
answer: Check trace ID, stack trace, deployment/config changes, downstream and DB errors before restarting.
interview: Preserve evidence and correlate the failure through logs, metrics and traces.

title: Prevent cascading failures
short: Use timeouts, bounded concurrency, circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding.
answer: Unlimited waiting exhausts threads/connections; isolation prevents blast radius.
interview: Use timeouts, bounded concurrency, circuit breakers, bulkheads and load shedding.

title: Blue-green deployment
short: Run old and new environments and switch traffic after validation.
answer: Rollback is fast, but database migrations must remain compatible during transition.
interview: Run old and new environments and switch traffic after validation.

title: Canary deployment
short: Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version before wider rollout.
answer: Use health and business metrics as rollout gates.
interview: Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version before wider rollout.

title: Distributed lock
short: A distributed lock coordinates exclusive ownership across instances.
answer: Leases/expiration and failure semantics are essential. Idempotency may be safer than locking.
interview: A distributed lock coordinates exclusive ownership across instances.

title: Strangler pattern
short: Incrementally replace slices of a legacy system.
answer: Route capabilities to new components, validate, then retire legacy paths.
followups: When is it better than rewrite?
interview: Incrementally replace slices of a legacy system.

title: Persistence context
short: It is the EntityManager-managed set of tracked entities.
answer: It provides identity semantics and dirty checking for managed entities.
interview: It is the EntityManager-managed set of tracked entities.

title: Entity states
short: Entities can be transient, managed, detached or removed.
answer: Lifecycle state explains persist, merge, detach and remove behavior.
interview: Entities can be transient, managed, detached or removed.

title: persist vs merge
short: persist makes a new entity managed; merge copies state into a managed instance and returns it.
answer: merge does not simply reattach the same object.
interview: persist makes a new entity managed; merge copies state into a managed instance and returns it.

title: Lazy vs eager fetching
short: Lazy defers association loading; eager asks for earlier loading.
answer: Lazy can cause N+1/LazyInitializationException; eager can over-fetch.
interview: Lazy defers association loading; eager asks for earlier loading.

title: N+1 query problem
short: One parent query plus one query per accessed association.
answer: Fix with fetch joins, EntityGraphs, batch fetching or projections.
code: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer
interview: One parent query plus one query per accessed association.

title: @Version optimistic locking
short: A version field detects concurrent updates.
answer: Hibernate includes the version in update conditions and increments it.
interview: A version field detects concurrent updates.

title: JPQL
short: JPQL queries entities and mapped fields rather than database tables/columns.
answer: Use native SQL when database-specific features or specialized queries are justified.
code: SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.status=:status
interview: JPQL queries entities and mapped fields rather than database tables/columns.

title: EntityGraph
short: It defines a use-case-specific fetch plan.
answer: It avoids making relationships globally eager.
interview: It defines a use-case-specific fetch plan.

title: Dirty checking
short: Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and synchronizes them during flush.
answer: Within a transaction, changing a managed entity can be enough.
interview: Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and synchronizes them during flush.

title: Spring Data JPA save()
short: save generally delegates to persist for new entities and merge for existing ones.
answer: New-state detection depends on entity metadata/state. SQL may be deferred.
interview: save generally delegates to persist for new entities and merge for existing ones.

title: flush vs commit
short: Flush synchronizes pending changes with the DB; commit finalizes the transaction.
answer: A flush can send SQL while the transaction can still roll back.
followups: Why can a constraint fail at flush?
interview: Flush synchronizes pending changes with the DB; commit finalizes the transaction.

title: Cascade types
short: Cascade propagates selected entity lifecycle operations.
answer: PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH and ALL are available. This differs from DB FK cascades.
interview: Cascade propagates selected entity lifecycle operations.

title: orphanRemoval
short: It can delete an owned child removed from a parent relationship.
answer: Use for composition-style ownership, not independent child lifecycles.
interview: It can delete an owned child removed from a parent relationship.

title: Optimize JPA-heavy endpoint
short: Measure SQL, remove N+1, paginate, use projections/fetch plans and indexes.
answer: Treat generated SQL as a first-class performance artifact.
code: SELECT new com.example.OrderSummary(o.id,o.status) FROM Order o
interview: Measure SQL, remove N+1, paginate, use projections/fetch plans and indexes.

title: LazyInitializationException
short: A lazy association was accessed after the persistence context was unavailable.
answer: Use explicit fetch plans and DTO mapping inside a clear transaction boundary.
interview: A lazy association was accessed after the persistence context was unavailable.

title: JWT structure
short: JWT commonly has header, payload and signature.
answer: Header has metadata, payload has claims, signature protects integrity/authenticity. Base64URL is not encryption.
interview: JWT commonly has header, payload and signature.

title: Authentication vs authorization
short: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions.
answer: Roles, scopes and policies are authorization mechanisms.
interview: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions.

title: CSRF
short: CSRF causes a browser to send an unwanted authenticated request.
answer: It is especially relevant to cookie-based authentication. CORS is not a general CSRF defense.
interview: CSRF causes a browser to send an unwanted authenticated request.

title: Password storage
short: Store passwords using adaptive one-way hashing with unique salts.
answer: bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 are typical choices. Never store plaintext or reversibly encrypted passwords.
interview: Store passwords using adaptive one-way hashing with unique salts.

title: OAuth 2.0
short: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access.
answer: Authorization Code with PKCE is common for user-facing apps. OpenID Connect adds identity.
code: Client -> Authorization Server -> Token -> Resource Server
interview: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access.

title: CORS
short: CORS controls whether browser JavaScript can read cross-origin responses.
answer: It is browser-enforced; server-side authorization is still required.
interview: CORS controls whether browser JavaScript can read cross-origin responses.

title: Refresh token
short: A refresh token can obtain a new access token without re-authentication.
answer: Refresh tokens need stronger protection, rotation and revocation strategies.
interview: A refresh token can obtain a new access token without re-authentication.

title: RBAC
short: Role-based access control grants permissions through roles.
answer: Roles map identities to authorities. Complex systems may need policies/permissions.
interview: Role-based access control grants permissions through roles.

title: Service-to-service security
short: Use encrypted transport, authenticated workload identity and least privilege.
answer: mTLS, OAuth2 client credentials or workload identity are common approaches.
interview: Use encrypted transport, authenticated workload identity and least privilege.

title: REST API security checklist
short: Check authentication, authorization, validation, TLS, secrets, rate limits and safe logging.
answer: Review broken access control, injection, token handling, request limits and dependency vulnerabilities.
interview: Check authentication, authorization, validation, TLS, secrets, rate limits and safe logging.

title: Reverse a string
short: Use StringBuilder.reverse() or a character loop.
answer: The straightforward approach is O(n). The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I can reverse a string using StringBuilder.reverse(), which is O(n). If the interviewer wants the algorithm without the library method, I convert the string to a char array and swap characters from both ends toward the middle.
problem: Reverse the given string and return the reversed value.
approach: Use StringBuilder for the simplest solution. For an interviewer asking for manual logic, use two pointers on a character array.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n) for the returned character sequence.

title: Palindrome check
short: Compare characters from both ends toward the center.
answer: Two pointers give O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I use two pointers, one at the beginning and one at the end. I compare the characters and move both pointers toward the center. Any mismatch means it is not a palindrome. This takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
problem: Check whether a string reads the same from left to right and right to left.
approach: Compare characters from both ends with two pointers. Stop immediately when a mismatch is found.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1) excluding the input string.
streams: A Streams solution can be written by comparing the string with its reversed form, but the two-pointer solution is preferable when discussing algorithmic efficiency.

title: First non-repeated character with Streams
short: Count characters while preserving encounter order, then select count 1.
answer: LinkedHashMap is important for first-occurrence order. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I preserve character order while counting frequencies. LinkedHashMap is important because HashMap does not guarantee encounter order. After counting, I find the first character whose frequency is one. The overall complexity is O(n).
problem: Find the first character that occurs exactly once in a string.
approach: Count each character while preserving encounter order, then select the first entry whose count is one. LinkedHashMap is useful because it preserves insertion order.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(k), where k is the number of distinct characters.
streams: Use chars().mapToObj(...).collect(groupingBy(..., LinkedHashMap::new, counting())) and then stream the map entries to find the first count of one.

title: Find duplicates using Streams
short: Use groupingBy/counting or a seen set.
answer: A seen set can detect repeats in encounter order; groupingBy is declarative. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I keep a set of already-seen elements. When add returns false, that element has appeared before, so I treat it as a duplicate. This gives average O(n) time and O(n) space.
problem: Find the duplicate values in a collection using Java Streams.
approach: Maintain a Set of values already seen. A value is a duplicate when add() returns false. Filter those values and collect them.
complexity:
Time: O(n) average
Space: O(n) for the seen set and result.
streams: Use a HashSet in filter: filter(n -> !seen.add(n)). This is a common interview pattern, but explain that the stateful predicate should be used carefully.

title: Maximum salary by department
short: Group by department and select max salary.
answer: groupingBy plus maxBy directly models the requirement. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I group employees by department and then use maxBy with a salary comparator for each group. The important point is that this returns the maximum employee, not merely the maximum salary.
problem: Find the employee with the maximum salary in each department.
example:
Input: IT: Arun 70000, Ravi 90000; HR: Bala 50000, Divya 60000
Output: IT -> Ravi, HR -> Divya
approach: Group employees by department and reduce each group to the employee with the highest salary.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(d), where d is the number of departments.

title: Group employees by department
short: Use Collectors.groupingBy.
answer: The result maps department to employee lists. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I use groupingBy because the requirement is to classify every employee using the department as the key. The result is a Map<String, List<Employee>> and the operation is linear in the number of employees.
problem: Group employees into lists based on their department.
example:
Input: Arun-IT, Bala-HR, Ravi-IT
Output: IT -> [Arun, Ravi], HR -> [Bala]
approach: Use Collectors.groupingBy with Employee::getDepartment as the classifier.
complexity:
Time: O(n) average
Space: O(n) for the grouped result.

title: Second highest distinct salary
short: Map salaries, distinct, sort descending, skip one.
answer: Distinct is required if 'second' means second distinct value. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I first remove duplicate salaries because the requirement says distinct. Then I sort descending, skip the highest salary and take the next one. If there are fewer than two distinct salaries, I return an empty result or handle it explicitly.
problem: Find the second-highest distinct salary from a collection of employees.
approach: Remove duplicates, sort salaries in descending order and skip the first value. In production code, if performance matters, a TreeSet or a single-pass approach can avoid sorting.
complexity:
Time: O(n log n) due to sorting
Space: O(n) for the distinct values.

title: Longest name in each department
short: Group by department and choose max by name length.
answer: Use groupingBy plus maxBy. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I group employees by department and compare the length of each employee name using maxBy. This keeps the solution concise while making the business rule explicit.
problem: Find the employee with the longest name in each department.
example:
Input: IT: Arun, Ravi; HR: Divya, Karthik
Output: IT -> Arun or Ravi depending on input lengths; HR -> Karthik
approach: Group by department and choose the employee whose name has the greatest length.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(d) for the grouped result.

title: Anagram check
short: Compare normalized character frequency maps or sorted characters.
answer: Frequency counting is expected O(n). Define normalization assumptions. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: For an efficient solution, I compare lengths and maintain character frequencies. Every character from the second string decrements the corresponding count. If a count becomes invalid, the strings are not anagrams. This is O(n) time.
problem: Determine whether two strings contain the same characters with the same frequencies.
approach: Normalize the strings if required, compare their lengths, then count characters in one string and decrement counts while scanning the other.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(k), where k is the number of distinct characters.
streams: A simple Streams approach is to sort both strings with chars().sorted() and compare arrays, but that changes complexity to O(n log n).

title: Missing number 1..n
short: Use a long sum or XOR.
answer: The sum formula is simple; use long to avoid integer overflow under larger constraints. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I calculate the expected sum from 1 to n and subtract the actual sum. The difference is the missing number. I use long if the range can be large. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
problem: Find the missing number from a sequence containing numbers from 1 through n with exactly one number missing.
approach: Use the arithmetic sum n*(n+1)/2 and subtract the actual array sum. For very large n, use long to avoid integer overflow.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1).
streams: IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n).sum() is readable, but it still requires iterating through the expected range; the arithmetic formula is simpler for this exact problem.

title: Word frequency with Streams
short: Normalize and group words with counting.
answer: Define case/punctuation rules before coding. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I tokenize the sentence into words and use groupingBy with counting. Function.identity() makes each word the map key and counting produces its frequency.
problem: Count how many times each word occurs in a sentence.
approach: Split the sentence into words and collect them with groupingBy and counting.
complexity:
Time: O(n) over the number of words
Space: O(k) for distinct words.

title: Merge two sorted arrays
short: Use two pointers and take the smaller current value.
answer: This is O(n+m) for new output. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: Because both arrays are already sorted, I do not need to sort again. I compare the current elements from both arrays, copy the smaller one and advance that pointer. This gives linear time.
problem: Merge two already sorted arrays into one sorted array.
approach: Use two pointers, one for each input array, and repeatedly copy the smaller value. Then append the remaining values.
complexity:
Time: O(m+n)
Space: O(m+n) for the merged array.
streams: Streams can concatenate and sort both arrays, but that costs O((m+n) log(m+n)); the two-pointer merge is the expected interview solution.

title: Remove duplicates from sorted array
short: Use a slow write pointer.
answer: Sorted input enables O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: Because the array is sorted, duplicates are adjacent. I keep a write pointer for the next unique position and scan with a read pointer. Each unique value is written once, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
problem: Remove duplicates in-place from a sorted array and return the new logical length.
approach: Use a slow pointer for the position of the last unique value and a fast pointer to scan the array.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1) extra.
streams: Streams can produce distinct values, but that creates a new result and does not satisfy an in-place requirement.

title: First duplicate element
short: Track seen values and return the first repeated value.
answer: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space; clarify what first means. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I scan in encounter order and store values in a HashSet. The first time add returns false, I have found the first duplicate. This preserves the required left-to-right meaning.
problem: Return the first element encountered whose value has already appeared.
approach: Scan left to right and maintain a HashSet. The first value that cannot be added is the first duplicate encountered.
complexity:
Time: O(n) average
Space: O(n).
streams: Use a stateful Set inside filter and findFirst, but a normal loop is often clearer for this requirement.

title: Intersection of arrays
short: Use a set for membership or a frequency map when duplicates matter.
answer: For sorted arrays, two pointers are another O(n+m) option. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I use a HashSet for constant-time average membership checks. Then I scan the second array and collect values present in the set. If duplicates must be preserved, I would use a frequency map instead.
problem: Find the common elements between two integer arrays.
approach: Put values from the first array into a set and scan the second array. For a unique intersection, add common values to a result set.
complexity:
Time: O(m+n) average
Space: O(min(m,n)) for the sets.

title: LRU cache concept
short: Combine O(1) hash lookup with recency ordering.
answer: HashMap plus doubly linked list is classic; LinkedHashMap can implement access-order behavior. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: An LRU cache removes the least recently accessed entry. In Java, LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true already maintains this order, so get and put are O(1) average. For a custom implementation, I combine a HashMap for lookup with a doubly linked list for ordering.
problem: Implement an LRU cache that evicts the least recently used entry when capacity is exceeded.
example: Capacity 2; put(1,A), put(2,B), get(1), put(3,C) => key 2 is evicted.
approach: Use LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true and override removeEldestEntry. This gives a concise Java implementation; a custom HashMap + doubly linked list is the common L3 follow-up.
complexity:
Time: O(1) average for get and put
Space: O(capacity).

title: Top K frequent elements
short: Count frequencies and maintain a min-heap of size K.
answer: This gives O(n log k) after counting. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I first count frequencies. Then I maintain a min-heap containing only the best k elements. When the heap exceeds k, I remove the smallest frequency. This gives O(n log k) after frequency counting.
problem: Return the k elements with the highest frequencies.
approach: Count frequencies with a HashMap, then use a min-heap of size k so the least frequent selected element is removed when the heap grows beyond k.
complexity:
Time: O(n log k) after counting
Space: O(n) for the frequency map and O(k) for the heap.
streams: A Streams solution can group and count, then sort entries by frequency, but the heap approach is preferable when k is much smaller than n.

title: Linked-list cycle detection
short: Use Floyd slow/fast pointers.
answer: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: I use two pointers. Slow moves one node at a time and fast moves two. In an acyclic list fast reaches null. In a cyclic list, fast eventually catches slow, so their meeting proves a cycle exists.
problem: Determine whether a singly linked list contains a cycle.
approach: Use Floyd’s tortoise-and-hare algorithm. Move slow one step and fast two steps; if they meet, a cycle exists.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1).

title: Binary search
short: Repeatedly halve a sorted search interval.
answer: Keep boundary conventions consistent and use overflow-safe midpoint calculation. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: Because the array is sorted, I compare the target with the middle element. If the target is smaller I search the left half; otherwise the right half. Each step halves the search space, so the time complexity is O(log n).
problem: Find a target value in a sorted array using binary search.
approach: Maintain left and right boundaries, calculate the middle index safely, and discard half the search space after each comparison.
complexity:
Time: O(log n)
Space: O(1) iterative.

title: Balanced parentheses
short: Use a stack to match each closing delimiter with the latest opening delimiter.
answer: The LIFO structure matches nesting naturally. The solution below is a complete, runnable Java program with imports, a main method, sample input, and the core implementation.
interview: A stack is ideal because brackets must close in reverse order of opening. I push opening brackets and validate each closing bracket against the stack top. At the end, the stack must be empty.
problem: Check whether an expression contains properly balanced (), {}, and [] brackets.
approach: Push opening brackets onto a stack. For a closing bracket, check that the stack is non-empty and its top is the matching opening bracket.
complexity:
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n) in the worst case.

title: How to start system design
short: Clarify requirements, scale, consistency, latency, availability and constraints.
answer: Restate functional requirements, estimate traffic/data, propose high-level architecture and drill into bottlenecks.
interview: Clarify requirements, scale, consistency, latency, availability and constraints.

title: Design a URL shortener
short: Store a unique short key to URL mapping and optimize reads with cache.
answer: Write persists mapping; reads check cache then DB. Discuss collisions, expiry and analytics.
interview: Store a unique short key to URL mapping and optimize reads with cache.

title: Design a rate limiter
short: Define allowance per identity using token bucket/sliding-window logic.
answer: For multiple instances, shared low-latency state or gateway enforcement may be needed.
interview: Define allowance per identity using token bucket/sliding-window logic.

title: Design notification service
short: Accept requests durably, queue work, deliver via provider adapters and track status.
answer: API + outbox + broker + workers + provider adapters; add retries/idempotency/DLQ.
interview: Accept requests durably, queue work, deliver via provider adapters and track status.

title: Design order management
short: Make order state durable and coordinate payment/inventory/fulfillment with local transactions.
answer: Order service owns state; outbox publishes events; Saga/state machine coordinates outcomes.
interview: Make order state durable and coordinate payment/inventory/fulfillment with local transactions.

title: Design file upload service
short: Use object storage, preferably direct signed uploads for large files.
answer: API creates signed URL; client uploads directly; async workers validate/process.
code: API -> signed URL -> Object Storage -> Worker
interview: Use object storage, preferably direct signed uploads for large files.

title: Caching design
short: Place caches at client/CDN/gateway/app/distributed layers based on need.
answer: Define key, TTL, invalidation, stampede protection and consistency.
interview: Place caches at client/CDN/gateway/app/distributed layers based on need.

title: High availability
short: Remove single points of failure with redundancy across critical components.
answer: Use multiple instances/zones, health checks and appropriate data replication.
interview: Remove single points of failure with redundancy across critical components.

title: CAP theorem practically
short: During a partition, you cannot guarantee both strong consistency and availability for every operation.
answer: CAP describes partition behavior; different operations can make different trade-offs.
interview: During a partition, you cannot guarantee both strong consistency and availability for every operation.

title: Database sharding
short: Partition data across nodes using a shard key.
answer: A good key distributes load and supports common access patterns; cross-shard queries add complexity.
interview: Partition data across nodes using a shard key.

title: Read replicas vs sharding
short: Replicas scale reads; sharding partitions data to scale capacity/write load.
answer: Replicas may lag; sharding complicates queries and rebalancing.
interview: Replicas scale reads; sharding partitions data to scale capacity/write load.

title: Eventual consistency in design
short: Reads can temporarily lag writes while replicas/events converge.
answer: Define acceptable stale windows and user-visible pending states.
interview: Reads can temporarily lag writes while replicas/events converge.

title: Capacity estimation
short: Translate users/actions into QPS, storage, bandwidth and peak requirements.
answer: State assumptions and use order-of-magnitude numbers.
interview: Translate users/actions into QPS, storage, bandwidth and peak requirements.

title: Backpressure
short: Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming consumers.
answer: Use bounded queues, flow control, batching, rate limits or load shedding.
interview: Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming consumers.

title: Observability by design
short: Design metrics, structured logs and trace context from day one.
answer: Include trace IDs, latency/error metrics, dependency timing and business counters.
interview: Design metrics, structured logs and trace context from day one.

title: Primary key
short: A primary key uniquely identifies rows and cannot be null.
answer: A table has one primary-key constraint, possibly composite.
code: CREATE TABLE student(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,name VARCHAR(100));
interview: A primary key uniquely identifies rows and cannot be null.

title: Primary vs unique key
short: Both enforce uniqueness; a table has one primary key and can have multiple unique constraints.
answer: Primary key columns are non-null. NULL semantics for unique constraints vary by DB.
code: ALTER TABLE student ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE(email);
interview: Both enforce uniqueness; a table has one primary key and can have multiple unique constraints.

title: Foreign key
short: A foreign key enforces referential integrity.
answer: It ensures references point to valid parent keys subject to null and action semantics.
interview: A foreign key enforces referential integrity.

title: Normalization
short: Normalization reduces redundant facts and update anomalies.
answer: Normal forms improve integrity; intentional denormalization can help performance.
interview: Normalization reduces redundant facts and update anomalies.

title: Indexes and write cost
short: Indexes accelerate reads but consume storage and add write maintenance.
answer: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE may update several indexes. Use actual query plans to justify them.
interview: Indexes accelerate reads but consume storage and add write maintenance.

title: Composite index
short: A composite index contains multiple ordered columns; order matters.
answer: Design it around common predicates and sorting. It is not equivalent to separate single-column indexes.
interview: A composite index contains multiple ordered columns; order matters.

title: WHERE vs HAVING
short: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped results.
answer: Use WHERE to reduce input and HAVING for aggregate conditions.
code: SELECT dept,AVG(salary) FROM employee WHERE active=true GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary)>70000;
interview: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped results.

title: INNER vs LEFT JOIN
short: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps every left row.
answer: A WHERE predicate on the right table can turn a LEFT JOIN into an effective inner join.
code: SELECT c.id,o.id FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id;
interview: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps every left row.

title: Window functions
short: They calculate across related rows without collapsing them.
answer: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, SUM OVER and LAG support analytics with row-level detail.
code: SELECT name,salary,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) rnk FROM employee;
interview: They calculate across related rows without collapsing them.

title: Find duplicate email/contact
short: Group by both columns and filter count > 1.
answer: SELECT email,contact_number,COUNT(*) cnt FROM student GROUP BY email,contact_number HAVING COUNT(*)>1;
interview: Group by both columns and filter count > 1.

title: Database transaction
short: A transaction groups database work with commit/rollback semantics.
answer: Transactions protect atomicity and consistency while isolation controls concurrency.
code: BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
interview: A transaction groups database work with commit/rollback semantics.

title: ACID
short: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability describe transaction guarantees.
answer: Atomicity is all-or-nothing; consistency preserves constraints; isolation controls concurrency; durability concerns committed data survival.
interview: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability describe transaction guarantees.

title: SQL deadlock
short: Transactions can wait cyclically for each other's locks.
answer: Databases may abort one transaction. Keep transactions short and use safe bounded retries.
code:
T1 locks A -> waits B
T2 locks B -> waits A
interview: Transactions can wait cyclically for each other's locks.

title: EXPLAIN / execution plan
short: It shows how the database plans to execute a query.
answer: Inspect scans, joins, indexes, row estimates and actual statistics where supported.
code: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42;
interview: It shows how the database plans to execute a query.

title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
short: DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE clears table contents as a bulk operation, DROP removes the table object.
answer: DELETE supports WHERE. Exact TRUNCATE behavior varies by database.
interview: DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE clears table contents as a bulk operation, DROP removes the table object.

title: View vs materialized view
short: A normal view stores a query definition; a materialized view stores results.
answer: Materialized views trade freshness and refresh cost for faster reads.
code: CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT id,name FROM customer WHERE active=true;
interview: A normal view stores a query definition; a materialized view stores results.

title: CTE
short: A CTE names a subquery for readable multi-step queries.
answer: WITH can support recursive queries where the DB allows them. Materialization is optimizer-dependent.
code: WITH high_salary AS (SELECT * FROM employee WHERE salary>80000) SELECT * FROM high_salary;
interview: A CTE names a subquery for readable multi-step queries.

title: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking
short: Optimistic locking detects conflicts; pessimistic locking acquires database locks.
answer: Version columns work well when conflicts are rare; pessimistic locking can increase contention.
code: UPDATE account SET balance=?,version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?;
interview: Optimistic locking detects conflicts; pessimistic locking acquires database locks.

title: Troubleshoot slow SQL
short: Inspect actual query, plan, indexes, locks, row counts and recent changes.
answer: Use EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE safely, inspect blocking and test targeted changes on realistic data.
code: slow query -> plan -> locks -> index -> re-test
interview: Inspect actual query, plan, indexes, locks, row counts and recent changes.

title: Class loading in JVM
short: The JVM loads, links and initializes classes as needed.
answer: Loading finds bytecode; linking verifies/prepares/resolves; initialization runs class initialization when required.
interview: The JVM loads, links and initializes classes as needed.

title: Java memory leak
short: Reachable objects that should have been released can still consume heap.
answer: Common causes include static collections, unbounded caches, listeners and ThreadLocal misuse.
interview: Reachable objects that should have been released can still consume heap.

title: ThreadLocal risks
short: ThreadLocal is thread-scoped, which can be risky in pooled threads.
answer: Remove values in finally where appropriate. ThreadLocal does not automatically propagate across executor threads.
interview: ThreadLocal is thread-scoped, which can be risky in pooled threads.

title: CompletableFuture
short: It represents a future result and supports asynchronous composition.
answer: thenApply transforms, thenCompose flattens dependent futures and allOf combines work.
interview: It represents a future result and supports asynchronous composition.

title: ExecutorService vs ForkJoinPool
short: ExecutorService is general; ForkJoinPool is optimized for work stealing.
answer: Choose based on workload and isolation; blocking I/O should not casually share a CPU-oriented common pool.
interview: ExecutorService is general; ForkJoinPool is optimized for work stealing.

title: Transactional method calling another transactional method
short: Propagation applies when the call crosses the Spring proxy boundary.
answer: REQUIRED usually shares; REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer transaction. Self-invocation can bypass interception.
interview: Propagation applies when the call crosses the Spring proxy boundary.

title: Transactional exception vs global handler
short: The transaction interceptor decides rollback; controller advice formats the HTTP response.
answer: A RuntimeException propagating through the transactional proxy can trigger rollback. Advice is not the rollback mechanism.
interview: The transaction interceptor decides rollback; controller advice formats the HTTP response.

title: Spring Boot startup
short: SpringApplication bootstraps the application context and infrastructure.
answer: Configuration loads, beans are discovered/created and the web server starts for web applications.
interview: SpringApplication bootstraps the application context and infrastructure.

title: Dependency Injection
short: The Spring container creates and supplies collaborators.
answer: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, supports final fields and improves tests.
code: @Service class OrderService{private final PaymentClient c; OrderService(PaymentClient c){this.c=c;}}
interview: The Spring container creates and supplies collaborators.

title: Spring bean lifecycle
short: Beans are instantiated, injected, initialized and eventually destroyed when applicable.
answer: Startup includes post-processors and callbacks such as @PostConstruct. Lifecycle is container-managed.
interview: Beans are instantiated, injected, initialized and eventually destroyed when applicable.

title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository
short: They are component stereotypes; @Repository also supports persistence exception translation.
answer: All can be discovered by component scanning. The annotations communicate architectural roles.
interview: They are component stereotypes; @Repository also supports persistence exception translation.

title: @RestController
short: It combines @Controller and @ResponseBody.
answer: Return values are serialized through HTTP message converters, commonly JSON.
interview: It combines @Controller and @ResponseBody.

title: Spring Boot auto-configuration
short: Boot conditionally configures infrastructure based on classpath, properties and existing beans.
answer: Conditional configuration provides sensible defaults and backs off when appropriate user configuration exists.
interview: Boot conditionally configures infrastructure based on classpath, properties and existing beans.

title: @Configuration vs @Bean
short: @Configuration groups bean definitions; @Bean registers the returned object.
answer: @Bean is useful for third-party objects or customized construction.
interview: @Configuration groups bean definitions; @Bean registers the returned object.

title: Spring AOP and proxies
short: Spring AOP commonly applies cross-cutting behavior through proxies.
answer: Transactions, security and caching can be proxy-based. Self-invocation can bypass advice.
interview: Spring AOP commonly applies cross-cutting behavior through proxies.

title: @Transactional propagation
short: Propagation controls participation in existing transactions.
answer: REQUIRED joins/creates; REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction and starts another.
interview: Propagation controls participation in existing transactions.

title: Transaction isolation
short: Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe.
answer: Isolation levels trade consistency and concurrency. Exact behavior is database-specific.
interview: Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe.

title: Global exception handling
short: @RestControllerAdvice centralizes exception-to-response mapping.
answer: It creates consistent HTTP error contracts across controllers.
interview: @RestControllerAdvice centralizes exception-to-response mapping.

title: @Valid
short: It triggers Bean Validation on a request object when constraints are present.
answer: Validate DTOs at the API boundary and map validation errors consistently.
code:
record UserRequest(@NotBlank String name){}
@PostMapping void create(@Valid @RequestBody UserRequest r){}
interview: It triggers Bean Validation on a request object when constraints are present.

title: Validation without @Valid
short: Yes; Bean Validation can be invoked programmatically or through method validation.
answer: Inject Validator for manual validation or use @Validated with method constraints.
interview: Yes; Bean Validation can be invoked programmatically or through method validation.

title: Spring Boot Actuator
short: Actuator exposes operational endpoints such as health and metrics.
answer: Expose only necessary endpoints and secure them.
interview: Actuator exposes operational endpoints such as health and metrics.

title: Externalized configuration
short: Configuration is supplied outside code so one artifact can run across environments.
answer: Properties, YAML, environment variables and other sources can provide values. Secrets belong in secret management.
interview: Configuration is supplied outside code so one artifact can run across environments.

title: Spring profiles
short: Profiles activate environment-specific configuration/beans.
answer: Useful for environment differences, not as a replacement for runtime feature flags.
interview: Profiles activate environment-specific configuration/beans.

title: Filter vs interceptor vs controller advice
short: Filters are servlet-level, interceptors are MVC lifecycle hooks, advice handles MVC-wide concerns.
answer: Choose based on lifecycle boundary: filters for low-level request concerns, interceptors for handlers, advice for errors/binding.
interview: Filters are servlet-level, interceptors are MVC lifecycle hooks, advice handles MVC-wide concerns.

title: Spring Cache
short: Spring Cache abstracts method-result caching.
answer: Cache keys, TTL, eviction and consistency must be designed.
interview: Spring Cache abstracts method-result caching.

title: @Async
short: It runs intercepted methods through an asynchronous executor.
answer: It is proxy-based and is not a durable job queue.
interview: It runs intercepted methods through an asynchronous executor.

title: Spring Boot starter
short: A starter groups dependencies for a capability.
answer: It simplifies dependency setup and works with Boot dependency management.
interview: A starter groups dependencies for a capability.

title: Troubleshoot slow endpoint
short: Measure latency, traces, SQL, downstream calls, pools and JVM behavior before changing anything.
answer: Use p95/p99, traces, SQL plans, pool metrics and deployment timelines to isolate the bottleneck.
interview: Measure latency, traces, SQL, downstream calls, pools and JVM behavior before changing anything.

title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP
short: All provide core compute, networking, storage and managed services; requirements drive selection.
answer: Compare ecosystem fit, skills, regions, security, cost and managed services.
interview: All provide core compute, networking, storage and managed services; requirements drive selection.

title: Horizontal vs vertical scaling
short: Vertical adds resources to an instance; horizontal adds instances.
answer: Horizontal scaling requires appropriate state management and traffic distribution.
interview: Vertical adds resources to an instance; horizontal adds instances.

title: Load balancer
short: It distributes traffic across healthy instances.
answer: It may perform health checks, L4/L7 routing and TLS termination depending on product.
interview: It distributes traffic across healthy instances.

title: Container
short: A container packages an application and dependencies while sharing the host kernel.
answer: Containers improve deployment consistency but are not identical to VMs in isolation characteristics.
interview: A container packages an application and dependencies while sharing the host kernel.

title: Kubernetes high level
short: Kubernetes orchestrates containerized workloads using desired state.
answer: Pods run workloads, Services provide stable networking and Deployments manage replicas/rollouts.
interview: Kubernetes orchestrates containerized workloads using desired state.

title: Readiness vs liveness
short: Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness controls restart decisions.
answer: A process can be alive but temporarily not ready. Avoid fragile deep liveness checks.
interview: Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness controls restart decisions.

title: Autoscaling
short: Autoscaling changes capacity based on workload signals.
answer: It can use CPU, memory, request rate or custom metrics; downstream bottlenecks remain possible.
interview: Autoscaling changes capacity based on workload signals.

title: Object storage
short: It stores blobs as objects addressed by keys.
answer: Use for documents/images/backups; store transactional searchable metadata in a database.
interview: It stores blobs as objects addressed by keys.

title: Infrastructure as code
short: Infrastructure is declared in version-controlled files.
answer: IaC improves reproducibility and reviewability while reducing drift.
interview: Infrastructure is declared in version-controlled files.

title: Secure cloud backend
short: Use least-privilege identity, encryption, secret management, private networking and audit logs.
answer: Prefer workload identities/roles over static keys and use layered network/application controls.
interview: Use least-privilege identity, encryption, secret management, private networking and audit logs.

answer: Java 8 brought lambdas, the Stream API, the new Date/Time API (java.time), default/static interface methods, and Optional. title: Explain JVM, JDK, and JRE.
short: The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the full toolkit for developers — compiler (javac), debugger, and other tools, plus the JRE. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is what's needed to run Java programs — the JVM plus core libraries, but no co
answer: The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the full toolkit for developers — compiler (javac), debugger, and other tools, plus the JRE. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is what's needed to run Java programs — the JVM plus core libraries, but no compiler. answer: The JVM divides memory into regions: heap (objects, shared across threads, garbage collected), stack (per-thread, holds method frames and local variables), metaspace (class metadata, replacing PermGen since Java 8), and PC registers plus native method stacks. answer: Heap (young generation — Eden + Survivor spaces, and old/tenured generation) holds objects. The stack holds per-thread frames with local variables and partial results. answer: It occurs when the JVM cannot allocate more memory in a given region because it's exhausted and garbage collection can't free enough space. title: Explain garbage collection in Java.
short: GC automatically reclaims heap memory occupied by objects no longer reachable from GC roots. Most collectors use a generational hypothesis — most objects die young — so the heap is split into a young generation (Eden + Survivor spaces, coll
answer: GC automatically reclaims heap memory occupied by objects no longer reachable from GC roots. Most collectors use a generational hypothesis — most objects die young — so the heap is split into a young generation (Eden + Survivor spaces, collected frequently with fast "minor GC") and an old generation (collected less often with a heavier "major/full GC"). title: What are the different garbage collectors?

title: Constructor injection vs field injection.

answer: Constructor injection passes dependencies via the constructor, making them final and impossible to construct in an invalid state — it also makes circular dependencies fail fast at startup and is easiest to unit test without a Spring context. Field injection (\@Autowired\ directly on a field) is more concise but hides dependencies, prevents immutability, and makes plain unit testing harder. Constructor injection is the generally recommended, more robust approach.

answer: GET retrieves a resource (safe, no side effects). POST creates a new resource or triggers processing. PUT replaces a resource entirely (idempotent). PATCH partially updates a resource. answer: PUT replaces the entire resource with the payload provided — fields omitted are typically reset/removed — and is idempotent. title: Difference between POST and PUT.

answer: POST is generally used to create a new resource (the server assigns the identity/URI) and is not idempotent — calling it twice can create two resources. answer: A resilience pattern that monitors calls to a downstream dependency; after a configured failure threshold is exceeded, it "opens" and fails fast (without even attempting the call) for a cooldown period, preventing a struggling downstream service from being overwhelmed further and protecting the caller's own threads/resources from piling up on slow failures. title: How do you handle failures in downstream services?

answer: Combine timeouts, retries with backoff (for transient failures), circuit breakers (to stop hammering a failing dependency), bulkheads (to isolate resource exhaustion), fallback responses/cached data where acceptable, and good monitoring/alerting so failures are visible quickly rather than silently degrading the system.
interview: Combine timeouts, retries with backoff (for transient failures), circuit breakers (to stop hammering a failing dependency), bulkheads (to isolate resource exhaustion), fallback responses/cached data where acceptable, and good monitoring/alerting so failures are visible quickly rather than silently degrading the system.

short: HikariCP is the high-performance JDBC connection pool that's Spring Boot's default. It's known for very low overhead (lightweight bytecode, minimal locking) compared to older pools, with tunable settings like \maximumPoolSize\, \connectionT
answer: HikariCP is the high-performance JDBC connection pool that's Spring Boot's default. It's known for very low overhead (lightweight bytecode, minimal locking) compared to older pools, with tunable settings like \maximumPoolSize\, \connectionTimeout\, and \idleTimeout\ that need to be sized carefully relative to expected concurrency and the database's own connection limits.

title: Explain thread pool sizing.

answer: For CPU-bound work, the optimal pool size is roughly the number of available CPU cores (more threads just adds context-switching overhead). For I/O-bound work, where threads spend most time waiting, a larger pool is beneficial — a common formula is \threads = cores \* (1 + wait\_time/compute\_time)\ — so the right size depends heavily on the nature of the workload and should be validated with load testing, not just guessed.

title: Explain CPU-bound vs I/O-bound tasks.
short: CPU-bound tasks spend most of their time actively computing (e.g. complex calculations, encryption), and are limited by processor speed/core count — more threads than cores doesn't help. I/O-bound tasks spend most of their time waiting on e
answer: CPU-bound tasks spend most of their time actively computing (e.g. complex calculations, encryption), and are limited by processor speed/core count — more threads than cores doesn't help. I/O-bound tasks spend most of their time waiting on external operations (network calls, disk, database) with the CPU largely idle during that wait — these benefit from more threads (or non-blocking/async models) than there are CPU cores, since threads are mostly waiting rather than computing.
interview: CPU-bound tasks spend most of their time actively computing (e.g. complex calculations, encryption), and are limited by processor speed/core count — more threads than cores doesn't help. answer: Redis is an in-memory key-value store commonly used as a distributed cache — shared across all instances of a horizontally-scaled service (unlike a local in-JVM cache), supporting TTL-based expiration, various data structures (strings, hashes, sorted sets) beyond simple key-value, and very low latency since data lives in memory rather than on disk.

answer: When a cache reaches its size limit, an eviction policy decides which entries to remove to make room for new ones — common policies include LRU (evict least recently used), LFU (evict least frequently used), and TTL-based expiration (entries automatically expire after a set time regardless of usage), chosen based on the access pattern of the cached data.

answer: The challenge of keeping cached data in sync with the underlying source of truth (the database) as it changes. Strategies include cache invalidation on write (delete/update the cache entry when the DB changes), a short TTL to bound staleness, write-through caching (updating cache and DB together), and accepting eventual consistency for data where brief staleness is acceptable.

answer: Restricting how many requests a client (or the system as a whole) can make within a time window, to protect against abuse and overload — implemented via algorithms like token bucket or sliding window, typically backed by a fast shared counter store (Redis) in a distributed system, returning a 429 status once the limit is exceeded.

title: Explain circuit breaker with a downstream payment service.

answer: If calls to an external payment gateway start failing or timing out beyond a configured threshold, the circuit breaker "opens," and further calls fail immediately (or return a fallback, like queuing the payment for later) without even attempting the network call — protecting the calling service's threads from piling up on a struggling dependency. After a cooldown, it allows a limited number of trial calls (half-open) to test if the gateway has recovered before fully closing again.

answer: Rather than retrying a failed call immediately (which can worsen an already-struggling dependency), each retry waits progressively longer — e.g. 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s — often with added random jitter to avoid many clients retrying in lockstep and causing a synchronized load spike ("thundering herd"), up to a maximum number of attempts.

answer: The gateway sits in front of backend services and intercepts every incoming request, validating the presented credential (e.g. a JWT's signature and expiry, or introspecting an opaque token against an auth server) before forwarding the request — so individual downstream services can trust the request has already been authenticated, often just reading pre-validated identity/claims passed via headers rather than re-validating themselves.

answer: The verifier decodes the token's header and payload, checks the signature against the issuer's public key (or shared secret) to confirm it hasn't been tampered with, checks standard claims like expiry (\exp\) and issuer (\iss\), and then trusts the claims inside (user id, roles) for authorization decisions — all without needing to call back to the issuing server for typical stateless JWT validation.

title: Explain OAuth2 authorization code flow.

answer: The client redirects the user to the authorization server to log in and consent; the server redirects back to the client with a short-lived authorization code; the client's backend exchanges that code (plus its client secret) for an access token (and often a refresh token) via a direct server-to-server call — keeping the actual token exchange off the user's browser, which is why this flow is considered secure for server-side web apps.

answer: Start with metrics/dashboards to identify what's actually slow (which endpoint, which downstream call) and when it started, correlate with recent deployments or traffic changes, drill into distributed traces to pinpoint which service/hop is the bottleneck, check resource metrics (CPU, memory, GC, connection pool saturation) on the suspect service, and reproduce/profile locally if needed before applying and verifying a fix.

short: Use the transaction's correlation/trace id to search centralized logs and the distributed tracing system across all involved services, reconstructing the sequence of calls and identifying exactly which service/step returned an error or time
answer: Use the transaction's correlation/trace id to search centralized logs and the distributed tracing system across all involved services, reconstructing the sequence of calls and identifying exactly which service/step returned an error or timed out, then cross-reference that service's own logs and metrics around that timestamp for the root cause.
interview: Use the transaction's correlation/trace id to search centralized logs and the distributed tracing system across all involved services, reconstructing the sequence of calls and identifying exactly which service/step returned an error or timed out, then cross-reference that service's own logs and metrics around that time

answer: Run \EXPLAIN\/\EXPLAIN ANALYZE\ to see the actual execution plan, check whether appropriate indexes exist on filtered/joined columns and whether they're actually being used, look for full table scans, N+1 query patterns, or unnecessary columns being selected, consider rewriting subqueries as joins (or vice versa), and verify statistics are up to date so the query planner is making good choices.

title: Explain how you would investigate high CPU usage in a Java service.

answer: Take a thread dump (or use a profiler) during the high-CPU window to see which threads are consuming CPU and what they're doing (e.g. a tight loop, excessive GC activity, inefficient regex/serialization), correlate with GC logs to rule out excessive garbage collection, and check for recent code changes or unusual traffic patterns (e.g. a hot endpoint being hit far more than normal) that line up with the onset.

title: Explain how you would investigate a memory leak in production.

answer: Monitor heap usage trends over time — a genuine leak shows a steady climb that doesn't recover after GC. Capture a heap dump (ideally two, to diff) and analyze it with a tool like Eclipse MAT to find which object type is accumulating and its retention path (what's holding a reference to it) — common culprits are unbounded caches, listeners/callbacks never unregistered, or static collections that keep growing.
interview: Monitor heap usage trends over time — a genuine leak shows a steady climb that doesn't recover after GC. Capture a heap dump (ideally two, to diff) and analyze it with a tool like Eclipse MAT to find which object type is accumulating and its retention path (what's holding a reference to it) — common culprits are unboun

title: Why is String immutable in Java?
short: String cannot be changed after creation; operations create new String values.
answer: Immutability makes String safe to share, enables string pooling, simplifies caching and hashing, and avoids surprising changes when a String is used as a map key. Its internal representation is private and String does not expose mutating operations.
followups: Why is String a good HashMap key?
mistakes: Saying concat changes the original String.
Assuming immutability means no new objects are created.
interview: String is immutable, which makes it safe to share and hash, supports the string pool, and prevents a caller from changing a value after it has been passed around.

title: Explain the String pool.
short: The JVM maintains a pool of canonical String literals so identical literals can share storage.
answer: A literal such as "java" is normally interned in the String pool. If the same literal appears again, the references can point to the same pooled object. new String("java") creates a distinct object, while intern() returns the pooled representation.
followups: Where is the String pool located in modern JVMs?
Why should == not be used for String content?
mistakes: Treating all Strings as pooled.
Using == instead of equals() for content comparison.
interview: The String pool stores canonical representations of literals. It reduces duplicate literal objects, but explicitly created Strings can still live outside the pool.

title: What is defensive copying?
short: Defensive copying protects mutable internal state by copying objects at boundaries.
answer: If a class stores a mutable List or Date supplied by a caller, the caller could otherwise mutate the class state. A defensive copy is made on input and often again on output. For modern Java, immutable collections can also help when the data itself is immutable.
followups: Why is returning the internal list dangerous?
mistakes: Only copying on construction but exposing the internal list.
Assuming an unmodifiable view always makes the underlying data immutable.
interview: Defensive copying prevents external code from changing internal mutable state. I use copies or immutable collections at API boundaries.

title: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
short: A shallow copy copies the outer object while nested references remain shared; a deep copy also duplicates the nested mutable state.
answer: For an object containing a mutable Address, a shallow copy can leave both objects pointing to the same Address. Mutating that Address then affects both copies. Deep copying duplicates the object graph that must be independently mutable.
followups: How would you deep copy safely?
Why can serialization-based copying be problematic?
mistakes: Calling clone() a universal deep-copy solution.
Ignoring cycles and shared references in object graphs.
interview: Shallow copy duplicates the outer object; deep copy duplicates the mutable nested state that should not be shared.

title: Explain covariant return types.
short: An overriding method can return a subtype of the return type declared by the parent method.
answer: Java allows an overriding method to narrow the return type covariantly. This improves usability because callers of the subclass can receive the more specific type without an explicit cast.
followups: Can parameters be narrowed when overriding?
How is covariance different from method overloading?
mistakes: Calling contravariant parameter changes valid overriding.
Confusing overload resolution with overriding.
interview: Covariant returns let an overriding method return a more specific subtype while preserving the parent contract.

title: What is the Java Memory Model?
short: The Java Memory Model defines how threads interact through memory and what visibility and ordering guarantees synchronization constructs provide.
answer: The JMM explains happens-before relationships. synchronized, volatile, final-field guarantees and concurrent utilities establish visibility and ordering rules. Without a happens-before relationship, one thread is not guaranteed to observe another thread's writes in the expected order.
mistakes: Saying volatile makes compound operations atomic.
Assuming CPU cache behavior alone defines Java semantics.
interview: The JMM gives Java its visibility and ordering rules across threads. I reason about shared state using happens-before rather than relying on timing or CPU behavior.

title: Why is i++ not atomic?
short: Increment consists of read, modify and write operations, so multiple threads can lose updates.
answer: For a shared int, i++ can read the same old value in two threads and both write the same incremented result. AtomicInteger provides an atomic increment operation using concurrency primitives.
mistakes: Calling i++ atomic because int reads/writes are atomic.
Using AtomicInteger without considering the larger invariant.
interview: i++ is a read-modify-write sequence, not one atomic action. AtomicInteger or locking is needed when multiple threads update shared state.

title: When should you use AtomicInteger versus synchronized?
short: AtomicInteger is useful for independent atomic state updates; synchronized is better when multiple variables or invariants must change together.
answer: Atomic classes provide lock-free-style atomic operations for specific state transitions. If a business operation requires checking and updating several fields consistently, a synchronized block or Lock can protect the whole invariant.
followups: Can multiple atomic variables replace a lock for every design?
mistakes: Choosing atomics for a multi-field invariant.
Assuming atomic means globally thread-safe for surrounding business logic.
interview: I use atomics for simple independent counters or state transitions. For a compound invariant, I prefer a lock around the whole critical section.
