title: What is ThreadLocal and when can it be dangerous?
short: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own value, but values can leak across reused thread-pool threads if not removed.
answer: ThreadLocal is useful for request-scoped context in synchronous code, but application servers reuse worker threads. If a large object or security context remains attached, it can survive beyond the request. Call remove() in cleanup code when appropriate.
followups: Does ThreadLocal work across async thread switches?
Why are virtual threads different for ThreadLocal usage?
mistakes: Treating ThreadLocal as global storage.
Forgetting cleanup with thread pools.
interview: ThreadLocal isolates values per thread, but pooled threads live for many requests, so I always consider lifecycle and cleanup.

title: What are virtual threads in Java 21?
short: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads designed for high-concurrency blocking workloads.
answer: A virtual thread is cheap compared with a platform thread and can be parked when it blocks, allowing the JVM to reuse carrier threads. They are especially useful for request-per-task applications that perform blocking I/O. They do not make CPU-bound work faster.
followups: Should CPU-bound work use virtual threads?
mistakes: Saying virtual threads are faster CPU threads.
Creating unbounded external resources simply because threads are cheap.
interview: Virtual threads improve scalability for large numbers of mostly blocking tasks. They reduce thread-management cost but do not remove CPU, database or downstream bottlenecks.

title: What is try-with-resources?
short: It automatically closes AutoCloseable resources when leaving the try block, including when an exception occurs.
answer: The compiler generates cleanup logic around resources declared in the try header. If both the body and close operation throw, the close exception can become a suppressed exception.
followups: What interface must a resource implement?
mistakes: Manually closing resources in a finally block when try-with-resources is clearer.
Ignoring close failures completely.
interview: try-with-resources gives deterministic cleanup for AutoCloseable resources and correctly handles exceptional paths and suppressed exceptions.

title: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?
short: Boot configures beans based on the classpath, properties and existing beans, using conditional configuration.
answer: Auto-configuration classes are discovered by Boot and use conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean and property conditions. User-defined beans can override many defaults because conditions back off when an application already provides a bean.
followups: How can you see why an auto-configuration matched?
How do starters relate to auto-configuration?
mistakes: Saying Spring Boot scans every possible library and creates every bean.
Assuming auto-configuration cannot be overridden.
interview: Spring Boot auto-configuration uses conditional bean definitions to provide sensible defaults based on the application environment and classpath.

title: Explain the Spring bean lifecycle.
short: A bean is instantiated, dependencies are injected, lifecycle callbacks run, and later destruction callbacks execute when the context closes.
answer: The lifecycle includes instantiation, dependency population, aware callbacks where applicable, BeanPostProcessor hooks, initialization callbacks such as @PostConstruct, and destruction callbacks such as @PreDestroy for managed singleton beans.
mistakes: Reducing the lifecycle to constructor plus @PostConstruct only.
Expecting every manually created object to receive Spring lifecycle callbacks.
interview: Spring manages a bean through creation, dependency injection, post-processing, initialization and destruction. Lifecycle callbacks apply to objects managed by the container.

title: What is the difference between @Value and @ConfigurationProperties?
short: @Value is convenient for individual values; @ConfigurationProperties is better for grouped, type-safe configuration.
answer: @Value injects individual property expressions. @ConfigurationProperties binds a related property namespace to a typed object, supports validation and is easier to maintain as configuration grows.
code:
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment")
public record PaymentProperties(String baseUrl, Duration timeout) {}
followups: How do you validate configuration properties?
How are environment variables mapped to properties?
mistakes: Using dozens of @Value fields for a large configuration object.
Ignoring startup validation for required configuration.
interview: For a few simple values @Value is fine. For structured application configuration I prefer @ConfigurationProperties because it is typed, grouped and easier to validate.

title: What is Spring Boot Actuator used for?
short: Actuator exposes operational endpoints such as health, metrics and application information.
answer: Actuator integrates operational information into the application. Endpoints can be exposed and secured selectively, and metrics can be connected to monitoring systems. Sensitive endpoints should never be exposed publicly without appropriate security.
followups: Which actuator endpoints are useful in production?
mistakes: Exposing all endpoints to the public internet.
Treating health as proof that every dependency is healthy.
interview: Actuator provides operational visibility. In production I expose only required endpoints and protect sensitive data and management operations.

title: How do profiles work in Spring Boot?
short: Profiles allow environment-specific beans and configuration to be activated selectively.
answer: You can define application-dev.yml and application-prod.yml and activate one profile at runtime. @Profile can also conditionally register beans. This keeps environment differences outside application code where possible.
followups: How do you activate profiles in containers?
mistakes: Hard-coding production credentials in profile files.
Assuming profiles are a security boundary.
interview: Profiles select environment-specific configuration and beans. They help deployment configuration differ without changing business code, but secrets still belong in a proper secret-management system.

title: How does @ControllerAdvice work?
short: It provides centralized controller exception handling across controllers.
answer: @ControllerAdvice applies exception handlers globally, while @RestControllerAdvice combines it with response-body behavior. A handler can map domain or validation exceptions to consistent HTTP responses.
followups: How do you handle validation errors?
What if two handlers can match the same exception?
mistakes: Returning stack traces to clients.
Putting business logic inside the exception handler.
interview: Controller advice centralizes API error translation so controllers stay focused on request handling and clients receive consistent error responses.

title: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
short: PUT generally replaces a resource representation; PATCH applies a partial modification.
answer: PUT is commonly designed as an idempotent replacement operation, although exact semantics depend on the API. PATCH communicates partial changes. The API should define validation and null/omission semantics clearly.
followups: How do you implement optimistic concurrency for updates?
mistakes: Saying PUT always means database update and PATCH always means one field.
Ignoring idempotency and concurrency semantics.
interview: PUT represents replacement semantics, while PATCH represents partial modification. I also define idempotency and concurrency behavior explicitly in the API contract.

title: How would you diagnose a slow Spring Boot endpoint?
short: Start with measurements across request handling, database, downstream calls, thread pools and serialization.
answer: I would correlate the request with logs and traces, inspect latency percentiles and identify whether time is spent in application code, SQL, remote calls, thread-pool queues or GC. Then I would reproduce the bottleneck and change one variable at a time.
followups: Which metrics would you inspect first?
How do you distinguish CPU from I/O latency?
mistakes: Optimizing code before measuring.
Looking only at average latency instead of percentiles.
interview: I first measure the endpoint end to end, then break latency down using metrics, logs, traces and SQL timings. The fix depends on the bottleneck rather than assumptions.

title: What is Spring application event publishing?
short: Spring events let components publish an application-level event and other beans react to it.
answer: ApplicationEventPublisher sends an event to registered listeners. By default listeners execute synchronously in the publishing thread. @TransactionalEventListener can align handling with transaction phases such as AFTER_COMMIT.
followups: How do asynchronous listeners change failure handling?
mistakes: Assuming events are automatically durable like Kafka messages.
Publishing an event and expecting it to survive process failure.
interview: Spring application events are in-process notifications, not a durable messaging system. For cross-service reliability I would use a broker and an appropriate delivery pattern.

title: How does @Async work?
short: @Async runs eligible method calls on a task executor instead of the caller thread.
answer: Spring intercepts calls to @Async methods and submits work to an executor. The caller can receive void, Future or CompletableFuture depending on the method signature. Proxy rules mean self-invocation does not trigger the interceptor.
followups: How do you configure the executor?
mistakes: Using the common pool blindly for all workloads.
Assuming @Async works for calls within the same instance.
interview: @Async moves work to a configured executor through Spring interception. I size and monitor the executor for the workload and handle errors explicitly.

title: How would you design API versioning?
short: Version APIs when breaking contract changes are unavoidable, while preferring backward-compatible evolution where possible.
answer: Common approaches include URI versions, headers or media types. The important part is a compatibility policy, deprecation period, documentation and tests. I avoid creating versions for every additive field change.
followups: How would you retire an old version?
mistakes: Versioning every minor change.
Keeping old versions indefinitely without ownership or telemetry.
interview: I prefer backward-compatible evolution first. For breaking changes, I use an explicit versioning strategy, support overlap, measure usage and communicate deprecation before retirement.

title: What is the persistence context?
short: It is the set of managed entity instances associated with an EntityManager, providing identity, dirty checking and lifecycle management.
answer: Within a persistence context, loading the same entity identity normally returns the same managed instance. Changes to managed entities can be detected during flush. The persistence context also coordinates writes and relationship handling.
mistakes: Calling the persistence context a database cache.
Assuming it is shared across all threads.
interview: The persistence context is a transaction-scoped or extended unit of entity management. It provides identity, dirty checking and coordination of persistence operations.

title: Explain entity states in JPA.
short: An entity can be transient, managed, detached or removed.
answer: A newly created object is transient. persist makes it managed. After the persistence context ends it can become detached. remove marks a managed entity for deletion. merge copies state into a managed instance; it does not reattach the same object in-place.
code:
Order order = new Order(); // transient
em.persist(order); // managed
em.detach(order); // detached
em.remove(otherManagedOrder); // removed
followups: When does an entity become detached?
mistakes: Saying merge makes the passed object managed.
Treating removed as immediately deleted from the database.
interview: I distinguish object state from database state: transient, managed, detached and removed describe how the persistence context tracks the entity.

title: What is dirty checking?
short: Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and generates SQL during flush without requiring an explicit update call.
answer: Hibernate keeps enough state for managed entities to determine changes. If a managed Order amount changes inside a transaction, flush can generate an UPDATE. This is why unnecessary entity mutation can create unexpected writes.
mistakes: Calling repository.save for every field change.
Assuming dirty checking runs continuously against the database.
interview: Dirty checking compares managed entity state with its persistence-context snapshot and synchronizes changes during flush.

title: What is orphanRemoval?
short: orphanRemoval deletes a child entity when it is removed from the owning relationship collection or reference.
answer: It is commonly used for dependent child records whose lifecycle belongs to the parent. It is different from cascade REMOVE: orphan removal reacts when the child is orphaned from the relationship, while cascade remove propagates parent deletion.
code:
@OneToMany(mappedBy="order", cascade=CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval=true)
private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
followups: Is it appropriate for shared child entities?
mistakes: Using orphanRemoval for entities shared by multiple parents.
Assuming it is just a database foreign-key option.
interview: orphanRemoval expresses ownership: when a child is removed from the parent relationship, Hibernate can delete that child record.

title: How does optimistic locking work in JPA?
short: A version column detects concurrent updates and prevents silent lost updates.
answer: With @Version, Hibernate includes the version in the UPDATE condition and increments it on success. If another transaction has already changed the row, the update affects no row and Hibernate reports an optimistic locking failure.
followups: How should an API respond to an optimistic locking conflict?
mistakes: Saying @Version locks the row physically for the entire transaction.
Ignoring conflict handling and retry policy.
interview: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are relatively uncommon. A version check detects stale updates and lets the application return a conflict or apply a domain-specific retry strategy.

title: What is the N+1 query problem?
short: One query loads a parent list and then one additional query executes for each parent to load related data.
answer: For 100 orders, loading orders once and lazily accessing customer data can produce one query plus 100 additional queries. Fixes include fetch joins, entity graphs, batch fetching or purpose-built DTO queries, depending on the use case.
code:
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.customer")
List<Order> findOrdersWithCustomer();
followups: Why can EAGER still produce poor SQL?
mistakes: Assuming EAGER guarantees one SQL query.
Fixing N+1 by making every relationship EAGER.
interview: N+1 is a query-pattern problem, not simply a lazy-loading problem. I choose fetching based on the use case and inspect generated SQL.

title: What is the difference between save and saveAndFlush in Spring Data JPA?
short: save participates in normal persistence-context behavior; saveAndFlush additionally triggers a flush immediately.
answer: save usually schedules the change in the persistence context and SQL may execute later at transaction flush/commit. saveAndFlush calls flush after saving, which can be useful when subsequent logic needs database synchronization, but it is not a commit.
followups: When can early flushing hurt performance?
mistakes: Saying saveAndFlush commits immediately.
Using it after every save unnecessarily.
interview: saveAndFlush forces synchronization of pending persistence changes with the database, but transaction commit semantics remain separate.

title: How would you handle bulk updates in JPA?
short: Use bulk JPQL/SQL for large updates when appropriate, but understand that bulk operations bypass normal entity dirty checking and can leave the persistence context stale.
answer: A bulk update can be much faster than loading thousands of entities. After it, clear or refresh the persistence context as appropriate, and ensure transaction boundaries are correct.
followups: Why can bulk updates cause stale entities?
When would JDBC batching be better?
mistakes: Expecting entity callbacks and dirty checking for bulk JPQL.
Forgetting to clear stale managed entities.
interview: Bulk operations trade entity lifecycle behavior for throughput. I use them for large set-based changes and explicitly manage persistence-context consistency.

title: What is the difference between lazy and eager fetching?
short: Lazy fetching defers association loading; eager fetching indicates the association should be available immediately, but neither alone guarantees an optimal SQL query.
answer: Lazy is usually safer for large relationships because data is loaded when needed. However, accessing lazy data outside a valid persistence context can cause LazyInitializationException, while eager mappings can over-fetch. Query-level fetch plans are often preferable.
mistakes: Making everything EAGER to hide LazyInitializationException.
Assuming LAZY means exactly one extra query every time.
interview: Fetch strategy is about when associations become available, not a guarantee about query count. I prefer explicit fetch plans for important read paths.

title: What is service discovery?
short: Service discovery lets services find healthy instances without hard-coding changing network locations.
answer: A registry or platform such as Kubernetes DNS can provide service locations. Discovery may be client-side or server-side. Health and lifecycle integration are essential so callers do not route to dead instances.
code:
order-service -> discovery -> order-service instance A
                              -> instance B
mistakes: Treating discovery as a replacement for health checks.
Hard-coding instance IP addresses.
interview: Service discovery decouples callers from instance locations. In container platforms, DNS/service abstractions often provide discovery without a separate registry.

title: Why are timeouts essential in microservices?
short: Without bounded timeouts, a slow dependency can hold resources until thread pools, connections and queues are exhausted.
answer: Every remote call should have a timeout appropriate to the business operation. Timeouts should be combined with bounded retries, circuit breaking and observability.
followups: How do you choose timeout values?
What happens if retries exceed the caller timeout?
mistakes: Relying on library defaults.
Setting a huge timeout to avoid transient failures.
interview: A timeout converts an unbounded wait into a controlled failure. I choose it from an end-to-end latency budget and downstream behavior.

title: How should retries be implemented?
short: Retries should be bounded, use backoff and jitter, and only target operations that are safe to repeat.
answer: Retrying every failure can amplify an outage. I retry transient network or service-unavailable failures with exponential backoff and jitter, cap attempts, and avoid retrying non-idempotent operations unless an idempotency mechanism exists.
followups: How do you avoid duplicate writes?
mistakes: Infinite retries.
Retrying validation or authorization failures.
interview: Retries are a resilience tool, not a default for every exception. I use bounded attempts, backoff, jitter and idempotency where writes are involved.

title: Explain the Bulkhead pattern.
short: Bulkheads isolate resource pools so one failing dependency cannot consume all shared capacity.
answer: Separate thread pools, connection pools or concurrency limits can isolate workloads. If the payment dependency is slow, its capacity limit prevents it from exhausting resources needed by unrelated operations.
followups: What metric tells you a bulkhead is saturated?
mistakes: Thinking bulkhead retries failed calls.
Creating many pools without capacity planning.
interview: Bulkheads limit blast radius by isolating capacity. They complement timeouts and circuit breakers.

title: What is idempotency in an API?
short: An operation is idempotent when repeating the same logical request produces the same intended outcome.
answer: For payment or order creation, a client can send an idempotency key. The server stores the key and result so a retry does not create a second business operation.
followups: Where should idempotency keys be stored?
What if two requests with the same key arrive concurrently?
mistakes: Equating HTTP POST with automatically non-idempotent business behavior.
Using a non-unique key across unrelated operations.
interview: Idempotency protects business operations from duplicate delivery or client retries. I enforce uniqueness at the appropriate scope and define what happens for concurrent reuse.

title: Explain the Outbox pattern.
short: The service writes business state and an event record in the same local transaction, then publishes the outbox event asynchronously.
answer: The transaction commits the order row and outbox row together. A publisher reads unsent outbox rows and sends them to Kafka or another broker. Consumers must still be idempotent because publishing can be retried.
followups: How do you avoid publishing the same event twice?
mistakes: Saying the outbox guarantees exactly-once end to end.
Deleting the outbox row before successful publication.
interview: Outbox closes the database-to-message consistency gap by committing the state change and event intent atomically. Delivery still needs idempotency.

title: Saga choreography vs orchestration?
short: Both coordinate distributed business transactions without a global database transaction; choreography uses events while orchestration uses a coordinator.
answer: In choreography, services react to events and emit the next event. In orchestration, a saga coordinator explicitly commands participants and handles compensations. Choreography can become hard to understand at high workflow complexity; orchestration adds a central workflow component.
mistakes: Calling compensation a database rollback.
Using choreography for a workflow with dozens of tightly coupled steps.
interview: A saga provides business-level coordination with local transactions and compensating actions. I choose choreography for simple flows and orchestration when workflow visibility and control matter.

title: What is eventual consistency?
short: Eventual consistency means replicas or services may temporarily disagree but converge if updates are successfully propagated.
answer: After an order is created, a read model or inventory service may lag for a short period. The design must define acceptable staleness and user behavior during that window.
code:
Order Service -> event -> Inventory
                 
                 read model catches up asynchronously
followups: How do you handle stale reads?
mistakes: Saying eventual consistency means data can be permanently wrong.
Using it without defining acceptable delay.
interview: Eventual consistency trades immediate global agreement for availability and decoupling. The system needs explicit rules for stale data and reconciliation.

title: What is distributed tracing?
short: Distributed tracing follows a request across services using propagated trace and span context.
answer: A trace represents the end-to-end request and spans represent work done by individual services or dependencies. Trace IDs let engineers correlate latency and failures across service boundaries.
code:
HTTP request
  traceId=abc
  Order span
    Payment span
    Inventory span
mistakes: Treating logs as a complete substitute for tracing.
Creating a new trace at every service instead of propagating context.
interview: Tracing shows the path and latency breakdown of a distributed request. It is especially valuable when one user operation crosses multiple services.

title: What is CQRS?
short: CQRS separates command/write models from query/read models when their requirements differ significantly.
answer: The write side handles business invariants and commands, while the read side can be optimized for query patterns. CQRS does not automatically mean event sourcing or separate physical databases.
code:
POST /orders -> command model
GET /orders?customer=42 -> read model
mistakes: Assuming CQRS is mandatory for microservices.
Equating CQRS with two databases in every implementation.
interview: CQRS is useful when read and write workloads or models have materially different needs. I avoid it when a simple CRUD model meets the requirements.

title: How do you prevent cascading failures?
short: Use timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding and sensible dependency limits.
answer: A downstream outage can otherwise cause request queues to grow and exhaust threads. Resilience patterns should work together and be observable.
code:
Caller -> timeout -> circuit breaker -> fallback
                    -> bulkhead limits concurrency
followups: Why can retries make an outage worse?
mistakes: Adding retries without limits.
Using a fallback that performs another failing downstream call.
interview: I prevent cascades by bounding waiting and concurrency, failing fast where appropriate, and isolating dependencies. Then I monitor saturation and failure rates.

title: How would you handle duplicate Kafka messages?
short: Consumers should assume at-least-once delivery and make processing idempotent.
answer: A consumer can store a unique event ID or use a business key with a unique constraint. The state change and processed-event marker should be committed atomically where possible.
followups: Does Kafka exactly-once remove all application duplicates?
mistakes: Assuming retries never duplicate messages.
Checking duplicates only in application memory.
interview: I design consumers for at-least-once delivery. Idempotency is enforced at a durable boundary, often with a unique key and transaction.

title: What is backpressure?
short: Backpressure prevents producers from overwhelming a consumer by controlling the rate or buffering of work.
answer: In streaming systems, a fast producer can create unbounded queues. Backpressure can use bounded queues, demand signals, rate limits or dropping strategies depending on business requirements.
followups: What should happen when the buffer is full?
mistakes: Assuming an unlimited queue solves throughput problems.
Ignoring memory growth.
interview: Backpressure makes overload behavior explicit. I choose bounded buffering, throttling or rejection based on whether data can be delayed or dropped.

title: What is OAuth 2.0?
short: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated access to protected resources.
answer: OAuth separates the client, resource owner, authorization server and resource server roles. Access tokens represent granted scopes. OAuth itself is not an authentication protocol; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer.
mistakes: Calling OAuth an authentication protocol by itself.
Putting sensitive data into access-token claims without need.
interview: OAuth 2.0 is primarily about delegated authorization. For user authentication and identity claims, OpenID Connect builds on OAuth 2.0.

title: Explain the Authorization Code flow with PKCE.
short: PKCE binds the authorization request to the client that initiated it, reducing code interception risk.
answer: The client creates a code verifier and challenge, sends the challenge to the authorization server, receives an authorization code, then exchanges it with the verifier. The server checks that the verifier matches the original challenge.
followups: Why is PKCE important for public clients?
Does PKCE replace client authentication for confidential clients?
mistakes: Sending the code verifier in the initial authorization request.
Treating PKCE as encryption.
interview: PKCE proves possession of a secret verifier during code exchange. It protects authorization codes from interception, especially for public clients.

title: What is CSRF and when does it matter?
short: CSRF tricks a browser into sending an authenticated request to a site where the browser already has credentials.
answer: It is mainly relevant when authentication is automatically attached by the browser, such as cookie-based sessions. A common mitigation is a CSRF token tied to the session plus appropriate SameSite cookie settings.
followups: Does a Bearer token in an Authorization header eliminate CSRF risk?
mistakes: Saying CSRF is solved by CORS.
Assuming every API needs identical CSRF handling regardless of auth mechanism.
interview: CSRF exploits automatically attached browser credentials. For cookie-based authentication I use CSRF protection; bearer tokens supplied explicitly by clients have different threat characteristics.

title: What is CORS?
short: CORS is a browser-enforced policy controlling which origins can make certain cross-origin requests and read responses.
answer: The server returns headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Preflight requests use OPTIONS for requests that require permission negotiation. CORS does not protect a server from non-browser clients.
followups: Why is allow-origin * problematic with credentials?
mistakes: Calling CORS a server-side firewall.
Allowing every origin with credentials.
interview: CORS controls browser cross-origin access. It is not authentication and does not prevent direct calls from non-browser clients.

title: How should passwords be stored?
short: Passwords should be stored using a slow password-hashing function with a unique salt, never reversible encryption or plaintext.
answer: Use a password hashing algorithm designed for credentials, such as Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt, with appropriate parameters. The application verifies the supplied password against the stored hash.
code:
String hash = passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword);
boolean ok = passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, hash);
followups: Why is SHA-256 alone inappropriate for passwords?
mistakes: Encrypting passwords when a password hash is sufficient.
Using fast general-purpose hashes for password storage.
interview: Passwords should be salted and hashed with a password-specific adaptive algorithm. The system stores the hash, not the original password.

title: How would you secure service-to-service communication?
short: Use authenticated identities between services, encrypted transport and least-privilege authorization.
answer: mTLS can authenticate both service endpoints and encrypt traffic. Alternatives include workload identity with signed tokens. Authorization should be based on service identity and required scopes or permissions, not simply network location.
code:
Service A --mTLS--> Service B
Authorization: Bearer <service-token>
mistakes: Trusting any internal network caller.
Using one shared credential for every service.
interview: Internal traffic is still untrusted from an authorization perspective. I use workload identity, TLS or mTLS, short-lived credentials and least-privilege policies.

title: How do refresh tokens improve access-token security?
short: Short-lived access tokens reduce exposure while refresh tokens allow controlled issuance of new access tokens.
answer: A refresh token is typically longer-lived and more carefully protected. Rotation and reuse detection can limit replay. Revocation and storage strategy depend on the client type and threat model.
followups: Where should refresh tokens be stored in browser applications?
mistakes: Making access tokens extremely long-lived.
Treating refresh tokens as ordinary API bearer tokens without additional controls.
interview: Refresh tokens let access tokens remain short-lived. Because refresh tokens are powerful credentials, I protect them, rotate them where appropriate and detect reuse.

title: What is RBAC?
short: Role-based access control grants permissions through roles rather than assigning every permission directly to every user.
answer: A user may have roles such as ORDER_VIEWER or ORDER_ADMIN. The application maps roles to permissions and checks authorization at the appropriate resource boundary.
mistakes: Using roles as the only authorization concept for complex resource rules.
Checking authorization only in the UI.
interview: RBAC simplifies permission management by grouping permissions into roles. The backend must enforce authorization regardless of client-side controls.

title: What is a composite index and how does column order matter?
short: A composite index covers multiple columns, and the leading column order affects which predicates and sort operations can use it efficiently.
answer: For an index on (customer_id, created_at), queries filtering by customer_id can use the leading portion efficiently. A query filtering only by created_at may not benefit in the same way.
code:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created
ON orders(customer_id, created_at);
followups: How would you choose index column order?
Can an index help ORDER BY?
mistakes: Adding every column to an index.
Ignoring write and storage costs.
interview: Composite index design follows actual query patterns. I consider equality predicates, range predicates, ordering and selectivity, not just individual column popularity.

title: What is a covering index?
short: A covering index contains all columns needed by a query, allowing the database to answer it from the index without fetching table rows in some engines.
answer: Whether an index is covering depends on the database and query plan. It can reduce random table access but increases index size and write cost.
followups: How do you verify a covering index is used?
mistakes: Assuming every index lookup avoids table access.
Over-indexing large tables.
interview: A covering index can satisfy a query from index data alone when the optimizer chooses it. I verify the actual execution plan.

title: What is a window function?
short: A window function computes a value across related rows without collapsing them into one row per group.
answer: Functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, SUM and LAG can calculate per-row analytics while retaining row detail.
mistakes: Using GROUP BY when row-level detail is required.
Confusing RANK gaps with DENSE_RANK.
interview: Window functions let me calculate rankings, running totals and comparisons while preserving individual rows.

title: What is a CTE?
short: A common table expression gives a query a named intermediate result, improving readability and enabling recursive queries where supported.
answer: WITH creates a logical query block. It can simplify multi-step transformations and recursive hierarchy traversal. Whether it is materialized or inlined depends on the database and optimizer.
followups: When would a recursive CTE be useful?
mistakes: Assuming every CTE is materialized.
Using CTEs without checking the plan for performance-critical queries.
interview: CTEs make complex SQL easier to structure and can express recursion. I still inspect the execution plan for important queries.

title: Explain EXPLAIN and execution plans.
short: An execution plan shows how the database intends to execute a query, such as scans, joins, sorts and index usage.
answer: EXPLAIN helps identify full scans, poor join order, large row estimates, expensive sorts and missing indexes. EXPLAIN ANALYZE, where supported, compares the plan with actual execution behavior.
code: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
followups: Why can an index still be ignored?
mistakes: Optimizing from SQL text alone.
Assuming an index is always faster.
interview: I use the execution plan to understand where database time and row processing occur. I compare estimates with actuals when the database supports it.

title: What causes a database deadlock?
short: A deadlock occurs when transactions hold resources while waiting for resources held by each other, creating a cycle.
answer: A common pattern is transaction A locking row 1 then waiting for row 2 while transaction B locks row 2 then waits for row 1. Databases detect cycles and abort one transaction.
code:
T1: lock(A) -> wait(B)
T2: lock(B) -> wait(A)
followups: Why must applications retry some deadlock failures?
mistakes: Saying deadlocks mean the database is broken.
Retrying without making the transaction safe to repeat.
interview: Deadlocks are cyclic resource waits. I reduce them through consistent lock ordering, short transactions and appropriate indexing, and I handle transient deadlock failures with bounded retries when safe.

title: What is database normalization?
short: Normalization structures data to reduce unnecessary duplication and update anomalies.
answer: First, second and third normal forms progressively constrain dependencies and repeating groups. Practical systems sometimes denormalize intentionally for read performance, but the trade-off should be explicit.
code:
Customer(id, name)
Order(id, customer_id, total)
-- customer data is not repeated in every order row
mistakes: Treating normalization as a performance rule.
Denormalizing without a consistency strategy.
interview: Normalization improves integrity by reducing redundancy. I denormalize only when a measured access pattern justifies the additional consistency cost.

title: What is keyset pagination?
short: Keyset pagination uses a stable ordered key as the cursor instead of skipping a large number of rows with OFFSET.
answer: For large datasets, WHERE created_at < :lastCreatedAt ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 can avoid scanning and discarding many preceding rows. The ordering must be deterministic, often using a unique tie-breaker.
code:
SELECT id, created_at, total
FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < (:createdAt, :id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;
followups: How do you handle duplicate timestamps?
mistakes: Using only a non-unique timestamp as the cursor.
Assuming keyset is convenient for arbitrary page jumps.
interview: Keyset pagination is efficient for deep scrolling because the database seeks from a cursor rather than skipping large offsets.

title: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
short: DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE removes table data in a database-specific bulk operation, and DROP removes the table object itself.
answer: DELETE can filter rows and typically generates row-level changes. TRUNCATE is generally faster for clearing a table but has database-specific transactional and identity behavior. DROP removes the schema object.
followups: Which operations can be rolled back?
How does TRUNCATE affect identity values in your database?
mistakes: Giving database-independent rollback claims.
Using TRUNCATE when row-level filtering is required.
interview: DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP have different scope and transactional semantics. For interviews I state that exact behavior depends on the database engine.

title: How do isolation levels affect concurrency?
short: Isolation levels define which concurrent transaction effects can be observed, trading consistency guarantees against concurrency and locking behavior.
answer: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but can allow non-repeatable reads. REPEATABLE READ provides stronger repeatability, while SERIALIZABLE provides the strongest standard isolation at a higher concurrency cost. Exact implementation varies by database.
code: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
followups: Dirty vs non-repeatable vs phantom read?
mistakes: Claiming isolation levels behave identically across databases.
Ignoring the cost of stronger isolation.
interview: Isolation is a concurrency contract. I choose the weakest level that satisfies business correctness, then validate the database-specific behavior and performance.

title: How would you find duplicate records?
short: GROUP BY with HAVING identifies duplicate key combinations; a window function can also mark individual duplicate rows.
answer: For duplicate emails, GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 identifies duplicated values. ROW_NUMBER can then select which rows to retain or remove.
code:
SELECT email, COUNT(*)
FROM student
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
followups: How would you delete duplicates while keeping one row?
How do you prevent duplicates after cleanup?
mistakes: Grouping by unrelated columns.
Cleaning duplicates without adding a unique constraint afterward.
interview: I first identify duplicate business keys with GROUP BY/HAVING, then use a deterministic rule to retain one row and add a constraint if uniqueness is required.

title: What is a container image?
short: An image is an immutable packaged filesystem and metadata used to create containers.
answer: A Dockerfile describes image build steps. Containers are runtime instances of images, with writable runtime layers and isolated processes. Images should be small, reproducible and free of unnecessary secrets.
followups: How do you reduce image size?
mistakes: Baking secrets into images.
Treating a container as a lightweight virtual machine with its own full kernel.
interview: A container image packages the application and its dependencies; a container is a running instance using the host kernel and container isolation.

title: What is a Kubernetes Deployment?
short: A Deployment manages a desired number of pod replicas and supports controlled rollouts and rollbacks.
answer: The Deployment describes a pod template and replica count. Kubernetes creates ReplicaSets and replaces pods to converge on the desired state.
code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: backend:1.2
mistakes: Exposing a Deployment directly as a stable network endpoint.
Assuming a pod IP is permanent.
interview: A Deployment manages application replicas and rollout state. A Service provides stable networking to the selected pods.

title: What is a Kubernetes Service?
short: A Service provides a stable virtual endpoint and load balances traffic to matching pods.
answer: Pods are ephemeral, so clients should not depend on pod IPs. A Service selects pods using labels and provides stable DNS and networking semantics.
code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  selector:
    app: orders
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
followups: How does service discovery work in Kubernetes?
mistakes: Treating Service as a process running inside the pod.
Selecting pods with incorrect labels.
interview: A Kubernetes Service gives stable discovery and routing to changing pod instances.

title: What is autoscaling?
short: Autoscaling changes compute capacity based on demand or resource signals.
answer: Horizontal scaling adds instances or pods; vertical scaling increases resources per instance. Good autoscaling needs meaningful metrics, cooldown behavior and protection against oscillation.
code:
HPA: desiredReplicas = metric / target
// Kubernetes adjusts pod count
followups: Why can CPU be a poor autoscaling metric?
mistakes: Assuming more instances always fix latency.
Scaling on a metric unrelated to actual bottleneck.
interview: Autoscaling adjusts capacity as demand changes. I choose the scaling dimension and signal based on the workload and verify that downstream dependencies can scale too.

title: What is a VPC or virtual network?
short: It is an isolated logical network in a cloud environment containing subnets, routes and security controls.
answer: A typical design separates public and private subnets, places load balancers at appropriate boundaries and keeps databases private. Exact components vary by provider.
code: Internet -> public load balancer -> private application subnet -> private database subnet
mistakes: Putting databases directly on public subnets without need.
Treating network isolation as sufficient application authorization.
interview: A cloud virtual network defines routing and network boundaries. I combine private placement with identity and application-layer authorization.

title: What is IAM?
short: Identity and Access Management controls who or what can access cloud resources and what actions are allowed.
answer: IAM typically uses identities, roles, policies and temporary credentials. Least privilege means granting only required actions on required resources.
code:
Role -> policy -> allow
resource: storage://orders/*
action: read
mistakes: Using root or administrator credentials for applications.
Granting wildcard permissions everywhere.
interview: IAM provides identity and authorization for cloud resources. I prefer workload roles and short-lived credentials with least privilege.

title: What is a managed database?
short: A managed database delegates operational tasks such as provisioning, patching, backups and failover to the cloud provider.
answer: Managed does not mean no responsibility. The application still owns schema, indexes, query behavior, credentials, data lifecycle and recovery objectives.
code:
Application -> managed PostgreSQL
                 provider handles patching/backups
mistakes: Assuming the provider guarantees application-level correctness.
Skipping backup restore testing.
interview: Managed databases reduce operational work but do not remove engineering responsibility for performance, security, backups and recovery testing.

title: What is blue-green deployment?
short: Blue-green deployment maintains two environments and switches traffic from the old version to the new version after validation.
answer: The inactive environment receives the new release. After smoke tests, routing changes to it. Rollback can be fast by switching traffic back, provided database changes are backward compatible.
code:
Blue: v1 <- traffic
Green: v2 <- deploy/test
Switch traffic -> Green
followups: How do you handle database schema changes?
mistakes: Ignoring database compatibility during rollback.
Calling a canary deployment blue-green.
interview: Blue-green reduces release switching risk by keeping old and new environments available. Database changes must support both versions during the transition.

title: How do you estimate capacity in system design?
short: Start with users, request rates, payload sizes and storage growth, then translate them into approximate compute, network and database requirements.
answer: I estimate average and peak requests per second, read/write ratio, data size per request, daily storage growth and retention. The goal is order-of-magnitude sizing that guides architecture rather than false precision.
code:
1M users * 10 requests/day = 10M/day
10M / 86400 ~= 116 avg RPS
Use a peak multiplier for capacity planning.
mistakes: Treating average RPS as production capacity.
Using unrealistic precision for uncertain assumptions.
interview: Capacity estimation is about making assumptions explicit and finding bottlenecks early. I calculate average and peak load, storage and bandwidth before selecting components.

title: What is caching and where can it be applied?
short: Caching stores reusable data closer to consumers to reduce latency and backend load.
answer: Caches can exist in the browser, CDN, API layer, service memory or distributed stores such as Redis. The design must define TTL, invalidation, consistency and cache stampede behavior.
code:
Cache miss -> DB -> set cache
Cache hit -> return cached value
followups: How do you prevent cache stampede?
mistakes: Treating cached data as always correct.
Adding caching without an invalidation strategy.
interview: Caching improves latency and reduces load, but it introduces staleness and invalidation complexity. I define the consistency and failure behavior explicitly.

title: How do you design a rate limiter?
short: A rate limiter controls request frequency using algorithms such as token bucket or sliding window.
answer: Token bucket allows bursts up to a configured capacity while replenishing tokens at a fixed rate. A distributed limiter needs shared state or a gateway that owns the limit.
code:
tokens = min(capacity, tokens + refillRate * elapsed);
if (tokens >= 1) { tokens--; allow(); } else reject();
mistakes: Using only local memory for a multi-instance global limit.
Returning an ambiguous response without retry guidance.
interview: I choose a limiter based on whether bursts are allowed and where state should live. For distributed services, the policy and shared state must be consistent enough for the business requirement.

title: How does a CDN improve a backend system?
short: A CDN serves cacheable content from edge locations close to users, reducing origin latency and traffic.
answer: Static assets are the simplest case, but CDNs can also cache selected API responses when semantics allow. Cache keys, TTLs, invalidation and authorization must be designed carefully.
code:
User -> Edge CDN -> Origin
             cache hit: response
mistakes: Caching private data publicly.
Assuming CDN removes origin scaling requirements completely.
interview: A CDN reduces distance to cacheable content and shields the origin. I pay particular attention to cache keys, authorization and invalidation.

title: How would you design a notification service?
short: Separate notification intent from channel delivery, use durable queues, idempotent consumers and provider-specific adapters.
answer: An application emits a NotificationRequested event. Workers consume it, select email/SMS/push channels, call providers with retries and record delivery state. A dead-letter path handles poison messages.
code:
App -> Event/Queue -> Notification Worker
                         -> Email Provider
                         -> SMS Provider
followups: How do you avoid duplicate notifications?
How do you handle provider outages?
mistakes: Calling providers synchronously inside the main transaction.
Retrying indefinitely and spamming users.
interview: I decouple notification delivery with durable messaging, idempotent processing and bounded retries. Provider failures should not block the core business transaction.

title: How would you design a URL shortener?
short: Generate a compact unique key, map it to the destination, cache hot mappings and handle high read traffic efficiently.
answer: The write path creates a unique ID or encoded sequence and stores the mapping. The read path checks cache then the database. Abuse controls, expiration and analytics can be separate concerns.
code:
POST /shorten -> key=abc123 -> DB
GET /abc123 -> cache/DB -> 302 destination
followups: How do you generate unique IDs at scale?
How do you prevent malicious links?
mistakes: Using a random key without collision handling.
Putting analytics synchronously on every redirect.
interview: A URL shortener is read-heavy, so I optimize lookup latency with caching and a compact key-generation strategy, while isolating analytics from the redirect path.

title: How would you design an audit logging system?
short: Audit logs should be append-oriented, tamper-resistant and correlated to actor, action, resource and time.
answer: Business services emit audit events with request and actor context. A durable pipeline stores them separately from mutable business data, with retention and access controls.
code:
Service -> Audit Event -> Queue -> Append-only Store
{actor, action, resource, timestamp, requestId}
followups: How do you prevent audit loss?
What data should never be logged?
mistakes: Logging secrets or credentials.
Relying only on application text logs for compliance records.
interview: Audit logging is a separate integrity concern. I capture who did what and when, make delivery durable, restrict access and avoid sensitive secrets.

title: What is a load balancer health check?
short: A health check determines whether an instance should receive traffic based on its readiness or health state.
answer: Liveness answers whether a process should be restarted; readiness answers whether it should receive traffic. A readiness endpoint should reflect the dependencies required to serve requests without becoming so strict that temporary issues cause instability.
code:
GET /actuator/health/readiness
200 -> eligible for traffic
503 -> remove from rotation
mistakes: Using liveness as a dependency health check and causing restart loops.
Making health checks more expensive than real requests.
interview: Readiness protects users from instances that are alive but unable to serve. Liveness is for process recovery; they should have different purposes.

title: Reverse a string without using StringBuilder.reverse()
short: Reverse characters with a two-pointer swap.
answer: Convert to a char array and swap from both ends.
followups: How would you reverse words instead?
mistakes: Using repeated concatenation in a loop.
interview: I use two pointers on a char array. Time is O(n). Space is O(n) for the array.

title: Check whether two strings are anagrams
short: Determine whether two strings contain identical character frequencies.
answer: Count characters in the first string and decrement counts for the second.
mistakes: Using a fixed array for arbitrary Unicode without stating the assumption.
interview: For ASCII input this is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

title: Find the first non-repeated character
short: Return the first character whose frequency is one.
answer: Count frequencies, then scan the original order.
followups: Can you solve it with streams?
mistakes: Losing original order when scanning only the map.
interview: Two passes give O(n) time and O(k) space for k distinct characters.

title: Find duplicate elements in an integer array
short: Return values that occur more than once.
answer: Track seen values and add repeats to a second set.
followups: Can you do it without extra space?
mistakes: Adding every duplicate occurrence.
interview: Average O(n) time and O(n) extra space.

title: Find the second largest distinct number
short: Find the second largest distinct value without sorting.
answer: Maintain largest and second-largest distinct values in one pass.
followups: How would you find the kth largest?
mistakes: Forgetting the distinct requirement.
interview: One pass gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Move all zeros to the end
short: Move zeros to the end while preserving non-zero order.
answer: Compact non-zero values then fill the remaining positions with zeros.
followups: Can you solve it using swaps?
mistakes: Changing the relative order of non-zero values.
interview: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Find the missing number from 1 to n
short: Find the missing value from 1 through n.
answer: XOR all expected values and all input values; equal values cancel.
followups: Why use XOR instead of the sum formula?
mistakes: Applying it when duplicates exist.
interview: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Find the maximum subarray sum
short: Find the largest sum of any contiguous subarray.
answer: Kadane keeps the best subarray ending at the current position and the global best.
followups: How do you return the subarray indices?
mistakes: Initializing best to zero fails for all-negative arrays.
interview: Kadane is O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Validate balanced parentheses
short: Check whether brackets are correctly nested and closed.
answer: Push openings and match each closing bracket against the top of the stack.
followups: Why use Deque instead of Stack?
mistakes: Checking only bracket counts.
interview: O(n) time and O(n) worst-case space.

title: Implement an LRU cache
short: Build a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used entry.
answer: LinkedHashMap can maintain access order and remove the eldest entry.
followups: How would you implement LRU from scratch?
mistakes: Forgetting access-order=true.
interview: This implementation gives average O(1) get/put behavior from LinkedHashMap. Production concurrency and distributed requirements need additional design.

title: What is service discovery in microservices?
short: Service discovery lets a service find another service dynamically instead of hard-coding host and port.
answer: A registry maintains service instances and their locations. A client-side or server-side discovery mechanism resolves a logical service name to a healthy instance. This becomes important when containers scale up, down or move.
code: Client -> service registry -> Order Service instances
followups: What is the difference between client-side and server-side discovery?
mistakes: Hard-coding pod IP addresses.
interview: Service discovery removes the need for callers to know physical instance locations. A registry or platform resolves the logical service name to an available instance.

title: Client-side vs server-side service discovery
short: Client-side discovery makes the caller choose an instance; server-side discovery delegates that choice to a load balancer or proxy.
answer: With client-side discovery, the client queries a registry and performs load balancing. With server-side discovery, the client calls a stable endpoint and the load balancer or platform resolves an instance.
code:
Client -> Registry -> choose instance
Client -> Load Balancer -> choose instance
mistakes: Treating service discovery and load balancing as exactly the same component.
interview: Client-side discovery gives the application more control, while server-side discovery centralizes routing and keeps clients simpler.

title: What is a circuit breaker and why is it needed?
short: A circuit breaker stops repeatedly calling an unhealthy dependency so failures do not cascade.
answer: It normally moves through closed, open and half-open states. After repeated failures the circuit opens and fails fast; after a recovery delay it allows limited probes in half-open state.
code: Closed -> failures -> Open -> wait -> Half-open -> success -> Closed
followups: How do you configure failure thresholds?
mistakes: Using a circuit breaker as a replacement for timeouts.
interview: A circuit breaker protects a system from repeatedly calling a failing dependency. It fails fast while the dependency is unhealthy and periodically probes for recovery.

title: Why should retries use exponential backoff and jitter?
short: Backoff spaces retry attempts and jitter prevents many clients from retrying simultaneously.
answer: Immediate retries can amplify load on a degraded service. Exponential backoff increases the delay after each failure, while jitter randomizes the delay so clients do not synchronize their retries.
followups: When should retries not be used?
How can retries cause a retry storm?
mistakes: Retrying non-idempotent operations blindly.
interview: I use bounded exponential backoff with jitter for transient failures and only retry operations that are safe to repeat.

title: What is the bulkhead pattern?
short: Bulkheads isolate resources so one failing workload cannot consume capacity needed by others.
answer: A service can maintain separate thread pools, connection pools or concurrency limits for independent dependencies. If one dependency becomes slow, its resource pool is exhausted without taking down unrelated traffic.
code:
Payments pool: 20 threads
Inventory pool: 20 threads
followups: How is bulkhead different from circuit breaker?
mistakes: Using one shared unbounded executor for every downstream call.
interview: Bulkheads limit the blast radius of a dependency failure by isolating resources such as threads or connection pools.

title: How do retries, timeouts and circuit breakers work together?
short: They solve different failure modes and must be bounded so resilience mechanisms do not amplify failure.
answer: A typical call has a short timeout, a small number of retries with backoff, and a circuit breaker around the operation. The total retry budget must fit inside the caller SLA; otherwise retries can make latency worse.
code: Request SLA 3s -> timeout 800ms -> at most 2 retries -> circuit breaker
followups: Where should the circuit breaker sit?
mistakes: Setting three retries with long timeouts that already exceed the SLA.
interview: Timeouts bound each attempt, retries handle transient failures, and the circuit breaker stops repeated calls when the dependency is persistently unhealthy.

title: What is idempotency in a REST API?
short: An operation is idempotent when repeating the same request produces the same intended business result.
answer: HTTP semantics alone are not enough for business idempotency. For operations such as payment creation, a client can send an idempotency key. The server stores the key and result and returns the same result for duplicate requests.
followups: How do you store idempotency keys?
What if two requests with the same key arrive concurrently?
mistakes: Generating a new payment every time the client retries.
interview: Idempotency prevents duplicate business effects when clients retry. A unique key plus durable storage and atomic handling makes the operation safe to repeat.

title: How would you design an idempotent payment API?
short: A payment API should atomically associate an idempotency key with the request and final business result.
answer: Persist a unique key scoped to the merchant or account, validate that a reused key has the same request fingerprint, process the payment within a transaction, and return the stored result for duplicates. For asynchronous providers, persist provider references and state transitions.
followups: How do you handle concurrent duplicate requests?
What if the provider times out after charging?
mistakes: Using an in-memory map as the only idempotency store.
interview: For payments I need durable idempotency keys, atomic uniqueness, request validation and explicit handling of unknown provider outcomes.

title: What is the Saga pattern?
short: Saga coordinates a business transaction across services using a sequence of local transactions and compensating actions.
answer: Each service commits locally and emits an event or calls the next step. If a later step fails, compensating actions undo the business effect of earlier steps. Saga can be choreography-based or orchestration-based.
code:
Order -> Reserve Inventory -> Charge Payment
Failure -> Release Inventory
followups: How do you handle compensation failure?
mistakes: Calling compensation a database rollback.
interview: A Saga replaces one distributed transaction with multiple local transactions and explicit compensation when a later step cannot complete.

title: Saga choreography vs orchestration
short: Choreography uses events between services; orchestration uses a central coordinator that directs steps.
answer: Choreography reduces central coordination but can become difficult to understand as event dependencies grow. Orchestration makes workflow state explicit in one coordinator but introduces another component that must be reliable.
code:
Choreography: OrderCreated -> InventoryReserved -> PaymentRequested
Orchestration: SagaCoordinator -> each service
mistakes: Saying choreography has no coordination; the events themselves coordinate the workflow.
interview: I prefer choreography for small, loosely coupled workflows and orchestration when the transaction has many steps, branching or compensation rules.

title: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
short: The outbox pattern atomically stores a business change and the event to publish in the same local database transaction.
answer: Instead of updating a table and publishing directly to Kafka in separate operations, the service writes the business row and an outbox row in one transaction. A relay later publishes the outbox event. Consumers must still be idempotent because publishing can be retried.
code:
BEGIN
UPDATE orders ...
INSERT INTO outbox ...
COMMIT
followups: How does CDC fit the outbox pattern?
mistakes: Assuming the database transaction can atomically commit with Kafka.
interview: Outbox closes the dual-write gap between the service database and a message broker by persisting the event alongside the business transaction.

title: What is change data capture (CDC)?
short: CDC captures database changes and makes them available to downstream consumers.
answer: A CDC connector reads database transaction changes, often from a database log, and publishes structured change events. It can feed search indexes, caches, analytics or an outbox relay without adding synchronous work to the request path.
code: DB transaction log -> CDC connector -> Kafka -> consumers
mistakes: Treating CDC as a replacement for business events in every use case.
interview: CDC observes database changes and can propagate them reliably, but business events may still be preferable when consumers need domain intent rather than row-level changes.

title: How do you prevent duplicate message processing?
short: Consumers should make processing idempotent because at-least-once delivery can produce duplicates.
answer: Store a unique event ID or business key with the processing result, or make the state transition naturally idempotent. The deduplication record and business update should be committed atomically when possible.
followups: What if the consumer crashes after the DB commit?
mistakes: Assuming a broker will never redeliver a message.
interview: I design consumers for at-least-once delivery and make the business effect idempotent, usually with a durable event ID or unique business constraint.

title: How do you preserve message ordering in Kafka?
short: Ordering is guaranteed only within a Kafka partition, so related events should use a stable partition key.
answer: If all events for an order use orderId as the key, Kafka routes them to the same partition and preserves their order there. Ordering across partitions is not guaranteed.
followups: Can multiple consumers process one partition concurrently?
mistakes: Expecting global ordering across a topic with many partitions.
interview: Kafka guarantees order within a partition. I choose a business key such as orderId so related events stay ordered while unrelated keys can scale across partitions.

title: What is a Kafka consumer group?
short: A consumer group is a set of consumers that jointly process a topic, with each partition assigned to at most one consumer in the group at a time.
answer: Consumer groups provide horizontal consumption. If a topic has eight partitions, at most eight consumers in one group can actively consume partitions concurrently. Different groups receive their own copy of the stream.
followups: Can two groups read the same message?
mistakes: Saying one partition is processed simultaneously by every consumer in the same group.
interview: A consumer group lets multiple instances share partitions for parallel processing, while separate groups independently consume the same topic.

title: What is Kafka consumer lag?
short: Consumer lag measures how far a consumer group is behind the latest available records.
answer: Lag can indicate slow processing, insufficient consumers, downstream bottlenecks or broker issues. I monitor lag together with processing latency and throughput instead of treating lag alone as the root cause.
followups: How do you reduce lag safely?
mistakes: Adding consumers when the topic has fewer partitions.
interview: Lag is the gap between produced and consumed progress. I first identify whether the bottleneck is consumer CPU, downstream I/O, partitions or broker health before scaling.

title: What happens during a Kafka consumer rebalance?
short: A rebalance redistributes partitions among consumers in a group after membership or subscription changes.
answer: A consumer joining, leaving or failing can trigger reassignment. During the rebalance, ownership changes and processing can pause depending on the protocol and client configuration. Commit strategy matters because records may be replayed.
code:
Consumer A: P0,P1
Consumer B: P2,P3
Join C -> reassignment
followups: How can you reduce rebalance impact?
mistakes: Assuming rebalancing means data loss.
interview: A rebalance changes partition ownership. Good consumer configuration, graceful shutdown and appropriate commit behavior reduce pauses and duplicate work.

title: At-most-once vs at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery
short: These describe whether messages can be lost, duplicated or processed with stronger atomicity guarantees.
answer: At-most-once may lose messages but avoids redelivery. At-least-once can duplicate messages and is common for reliable processing. Exactly-once requires carefully scoped transactional semantics and still needs business-level reasoning across external systems.
code:
At-most-once: commit -> process
At-least-once: process -> commit
followups: Why is exactly-once difficult end to end?
How do you design for at-least-once?
mistakes: Calling Kafka exactly-once equivalent to exactly-once business effects across databases and APIs.
interview: I usually design business consumers for at-least-once delivery with idempotent effects. Exactly-once can be achieved in bounded systems but is not a magic end-to-end property.

title: How do you handle poison messages in Kafka?
short: A poison message repeatedly fails processing and can block progress if it is not isolated.
answer: Use bounded retries, then route the failed record to a dead-letter topic or quarantine mechanism with enough metadata for investigation. The consumer should commit or otherwise advance according to a deliberate failure policy so one bad record does not cause an infinite retry loop.
followups: Should DLT messages be retried automatically?
mistakes: Infinite immediate retries on the main topic.
interview: I use bounded retries and a dead-letter path for poison messages, preserving the original payload, error, attempt count and correlation information.

title: What is a dead-letter queue or topic?
short: A dead-letter destination stores messages that cannot be processed successfully after the configured retry policy.
answer: It isolates bad messages from the normal flow while preserving them for investigation or controlled replay. The DLQ should have monitoring, retention and an operational replay strategy.
followups: How do you replay a DLQ safely?
Should every exception go to DLQ?
mistakes: Treating DLQ as permanent data deletion.
interview: A DLQ is a controlled quarantine for failed messages. It should be observable and replayable after the underlying problem is fixed.

title: What is backpressure in event-driven systems?
short: Backpressure prevents producers or upstream work from overwhelming a slower consumer.
answer: Controls include bounded queues, consumer concurrency limits, rate limiting, broker retention, flow control and load shedding. The right choice depends on whether data may be delayed, dropped or must be durably buffered.
code:
Producer rate: 10k/s
Consumer capacity: 5k/s
Need buffering or throttling
followups: How does Kafka help absorb bursts?
What if the backlog never drains?
mistakes: Using unbounded in-memory queues.
interview: Backpressure keeps a fast producer from exhausting downstream resources. I use bounded buffering and explicit policies for delay, throttling or load shedding.

title: How would you design an order event flow for reliability?
short: A reliable order flow uses durable state, transactional event publication, idempotent consumers and observable retry paths.
answer: Create the order and outbox event atomically. Publish to Kafka, partition by orderId, consume with idempotent inventory/payment handlers, use bounded retries and DLT, and expose correlation IDs and lag metrics.
followups: How do you recover from duplicate events?
What if Kafka is temporarily unavailable?
mistakes: Publishing directly after the DB commit without an outbox.
interview: I would use an outbox for atomic local persistence, Kafka keyed by orderId for ordering, idempotent consumers and explicit retry/DLT handling.

title: What are correlation IDs and why are they useful?
short: A correlation ID is a stable request identifier propagated across logs and downstream calls.
answer: When a request crosses several services, the same correlation or trace identifier lets operators search related logs quickly. It should not be treated as an authentication credential or sensitive data container.
mistakes: Generating a new ID at every service without preserving the incoming context.
interview: Correlation IDs provide a simple way to connect logs across services. In modern tracing systems, trace IDs can serve a similar purpose with richer context.

title: What are the four golden signals?
short: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
answer: They provide a compact view of service health: request latency, request volume, error rate and how close resources are to capacity. They complement application-specific business metrics.
followups: What business metrics would you add?
How do you alert on latency?
mistakes: Monitoring CPU alone as service health.
interview: The golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. They help detect user-visible degradation and resource pressure.

title: Liveness vs readiness probes in Kubernetes
short: Liveness asks whether a container should be restarted; readiness asks whether it should receive traffic.
answer: A readiness failure should remove the instance from service without necessarily restarting it. Liveness should detect an unrecoverable process state and be conservative to avoid restart loops.
followups: Why should liveness not depend on a database?
mistakes: Using a slow dependency check for liveness.
interview: Readiness controls traffic eligibility, while liveness controls restart decisions. I keep liveness lightweight so a temporary dependency outage does not cause restart storms.

title: What is graceful shutdown in a microservice?
short: Graceful shutdown stops new work, lets in-flight work finish within a deadline and closes resources cleanly.
answer: On termination, the instance should be removed from service discovery/load balancing, stop accepting new requests, finish or cancel active work, commit/rollback transactions and close consumers or connections.
followups: Why is readiness important during shutdown?
How do you handle long-running requests?
mistakes: Immediately killing the process on deployment.
interview: Graceful shutdown prevents dropped in-flight requests and partial work by draining traffic before the process exits.

title: How do you achieve zero-downtime deployments?
short: Zero-downtime deployment keeps enough healthy capacity available while replacing old instances.
answer: Use rolling or blue-green deployment, readiness checks, backward-compatible API/database changes, connection draining and fast rollback. Database migrations should follow an expand-and-contract strategy when schemas must coexist across versions.
code: v1 + v2 -> migrate -> switch -> remove v1
followups: How do you roll back a database change?
mistakes: Deploying a breaking schema and application change simultaneously.
interview: I combine rolling or blue-green deployment with readiness, graceful shutdown and backward-compatible schema changes so old and new versions can coexist during rollout.

title: How do you make database schema changes safe across microservice deployments?
short: Schema changes should be backward compatible while multiple application versions may run during deployment.
answer: Use expand-and-contract: add nullable/new structures first, deploy code that can read both forms, backfill data, switch writes, then remove the old structure after all old instances are gone.
code: 1 add column -> 2 dual read/write -> 3 backfill -> 4 switch -> 5 remove
followups: How do you handle renaming a column?
Why can a direct DROP break rolling deployments?
mistakes: Assuming deployment is instantaneous.
interview: During rolling deployments, old and new application versions can coexist, so database changes must be compatible with both.

title: What is a service mesh?
short: A service mesh provides infrastructure-level communication features between services, often through sidecars or ambient proxies.
answer: It can provide mTLS, traffic routing, retries, telemetry and policy without putting every networking concern into application code. It also adds operational complexity and another layer to debug.
code: Service A -> proxy -> proxy -> Service B
followups: When would you avoid a service mesh?
mistakes: Assuming a mesh removes all application-level resilience decisions.
interview: A service mesh handles common service-to-service networking concerns consistently, but it does not replace domain logic or all application resilience design.

title: How do you avoid a single point of failure in an API Gateway?
short: Run multiple gateway instances behind a highly available load balancer and keep gateway state external or stateless where possible.
answer: Gateway instances should be horizontally scalable. Authentication metadata, rate-limit state or sessions that must be shared should use a resilient external store or distributed mechanism.
followups: What if the gateway itself is overloaded?
How do you deploy gateway configuration safely?
mistakes: Running one gateway instance because it is stateless.
interview: I remove gateway single points of failure through multiple instances, health checks, horizontal scaling and externalized shared state.

title: How do you prevent cascading failures in microservices?
short: Cascading failures occur when one slow or failing dependency consumes resources across callers until the whole system degrades.
answer: Use timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, concurrency limits, load shedding, caching where appropriate and graceful degradation. Monitor dependency latency and saturation so protection activates before the caller is exhausted.
code: A slow B -> A threads blocked -> A fails -> upstream retries A
followups: Why can retries worsen cascading failures?
mistakes: Adding retries everywhere without budgets.
interview: Cascading failures are controlled by limiting dependency impact: short timeouts, bounded retries, isolation, circuit breaking and graceful degradation.

title: How do you handle partial failure in a distributed workflow?
short: Partial failure means some steps succeed while others fail or become unknown.
answer: Persist workflow state, use idempotent commands, explicit statuses and compensating actions where appropriate. For external systems, design for unknown outcomes and reconciliation rather than assuming timeout means failure.
followups: How do you handle an unknown payment result?
mistakes: Treating a timeout as proof that the operation did not happen.
interview: In distributed workflows, a timeout can mean unknown outcome. I persist state, use idempotency and reconciliation to converge the workflow safely.

title: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous communication?
short: Synchronous communication waits for an immediate response; asynchronous communication decouples sender and receiver in time.
answer: REST/gRPC is commonly synchronous and useful when the caller needs an immediate result. Messaging is useful for long-running, bursty or independently scalable workflows, but introduces eventual consistency and operational complexity.
code:
Sync: A -> B -> response
Async: A -> broker -> B
followups: How do you expose async status to clients?
mistakes: Using async messaging for every CRUD call.
interview: I choose synchronous calls when the caller needs an immediate answer and asynchronous messaging when decoupling, buffering or independent processing is more valuable.

title: REST vs gRPC for microservice communication
