short: Model the workflow as explicit states with local transactions, durable events, idempotency and compensations.
answer: Order service persists its state and an outbox event. Payment and inventory own their local transactions. A saga coordinates progress and compensation when a step fails.
followups: How do you recover a stuck saga?
mistakes: Treating the workflow as one database transaction.
interview: I avoid distributed ACID transactions. Each service owns its data, events connect local commits, and compensations handle partial failure.

title: How do you prevent retry storms?
short: Use bounded retries, exponential backoff, jitter, retry budgets and a total deadline.
answer: Nested retries multiply traffic. Retry only transient failures, preferably at one appropriate layer, and stop when the request deadline is exhausted.
followups: How does idempotency interact with retries?
mistakes: Retrying at every service layer.
interview: Retries must fit inside a latency budget and be safe for the operation. I also monitor retry volume separately from request volume.

title: How do you design a distributed rate limiter?
short: Use a shared atomic algorithm such as token bucket with per-client or per-tenant state.
answer: Redis or another shared store can hold tokens and refill time, updated atomically. Define fail-open/closed behavior and expose 429 responses.
mistakes: Using local counters in a horizontally scaled service.
interview: I choose token bucket when bursts are allowed, keep state shared across instances and protect the limiter store with timeouts.

title: How do you handle Kafka schema evolution safely?
short: Make event changes backward/forward compatible and roll out consumers before producers when needed.
answer: Prefer additive fields and tolerant readers. Use explicit event versions when semantics change and enforce compatibility through a schema registry where appropriate.
code: OrderCreated v2 { orderId, customerId, optional priority }
followups: When do you version an event?
mistakes: Removing or renaming fields immediately.
interview: I design events as long-lived contracts. Old and new consumers must coexist during deployment.

title: Explain the outbox pattern and its limits
short: Outbox closes the database-to-message dual-write gap but still requires idempotent delivery.
answer: Business data and an outbox row commit in one local transaction. A relay publishes later. Publishing can be duplicated, so consumers must tolerate redelivery and the relay needs retry/cleanup.
code: INSERT business row; INSERT outbox row; COMMIT;
followups: How do you clean outbox rows?
mistakes: Claiming outbox guarantees exactly-once end to end.
interview: Outbox gives a durable handoff from DB to broker, not magical exactly-once business processing.

title: How do you troubleshoot Kafka consumer lag?
short: Inspect partition-level lag, processing latency, rebalance rate, downstream latency and partition/consumer capacity.
answer: If one partition is hot, adding consumers may not help. Check max poll settings, batch size, consumer throughput and broker health.
code: metrics: lag, records/sec, processing ms, rebalances
mistakes: Scaling consumers without checking partition distribution.
interview: I first determine whether lag is uniform or concentrated. Then I identify whether the bottleneck is partitions, consumer code or downstream I/O.

title: How do you guarantee ordering in Kafka where it matters?
short: Use a stable partition key so related events land in the same partition and process that partition sequentially.
answer: Kafka ordering is per partition. Using orderId as the key keeps an order events events together. Global ordering is expensive and usually unnecessary.
followups: What if one key is hot?
Can one partition be processed concurrently?
mistakes: Claiming a topic is globally ordered.
interview: I promise only partition ordering. For order-specific ordering, orderId is the partition key and consumers process the partition in sequence.

title: How do you design a poison-message/DLT strategy?
short: Bound transient retries, preserve diagnostic metadata and provide controlled replay.
answer: After retry exhaustion, publish to a DLT with original topic/partition/offset, exception and trace metadata. Replay only after fixing the cause and ensure idempotency.
code: DLT metadata: topic, partition, offset, error, traceId
mistakes: Dropping failed messages silently.
interview: A DLT is a recovery mechanism, not a trash bin. I alert on growth and replay deliberately.

title: How do you safely use distributed locks?
short: Prefer idempotency or database constraints; if a lock is required, use leases and fencing.
answer: A lease can expire while a stale holder continues running. A fencing token lets the resource reject operations from an old holder.
mistakes: Assuming the lock holder is always current.
interview: Distributed locks are not automatically safe under partitions. I use them only when simpler ownership or uniqueness mechanisms cannot solve the problem.

title: How do you handle partial failure in fan-out requests?
short: Classify dependencies as required or optional and use bounded parallelism plus per-call deadlines.
answer: Optional dependency failures can produce partial results; required failures fail the request. Bound fan-out so concurrency does not exhaust threads or downstream quotas.
followups: When should you cache fan-out data?
mistakes: Calling every dependency serially with one large timeout.
interview: I use concurrency to reduce latency but make failure policy explicit and keep the fan-out within a resource budget.

title: How do you design zero-downtime database migrations in microservices?
short: Use expand-and-contract and keep old/new application versions compatible.
answer: Add new schema elements first, deploy dual-compatible code, backfill, switch reads/writes, then remove old elements after rollout completion.
mistakes: Combining destructive schema changes with the code release.
interview: Schema evolution is part of distributed deployment. Compatibility must hold while multiple service versions run simultaneously.

title: How do you choose REST vs messaging?
short: Use synchronous communication when the caller needs an immediate result; messaging when buffering, decoupling or eventual consistency are valuable.
answer: REST creates temporal coupling; messaging creates durable asynchronous handoff. Many real workflows combine both.
followups: How do you trace async flows?
mistakes: Using messaging for every request/response.
interview: I choose based on latency, coupling, failure and consistency requirements rather than using messaging everywhere.

title: How do you design multi-region active-active services?
short: Design the data consistency and conflict model first, then route stateless compute accordingly.
answer: Choose single-writer, region-local writes or multi-writer semantics. Define replication lag, conflict resolution, global IDs and failover.
code: Region A/B -> regional traffic; writes follow explicit consistency policy
followups: How do you handle split brain?
mistakes: Assuming replication automatically resolves write conflicts.
interview: Active-active is mainly a data problem. Two application clusters do not create an active-active system unless writes and failover are well defined.

title: How do you design tenant isolation in microservices?
short: Make tenant identity an end-to-end invariant across authorization, data, cache and resource quotas.
answer: Derive tenant from trusted identity, enforce it in queries, namespace caches and apply per-tenant limits. Test cross-tenant access explicitly.
mistakes: Trusting client-supplied tenantId.
interview: Tenant isolation cannot depend on a single controller check; the data boundary must enforce it too.

title: How do you handle backpressure in event consumers?
short: Bound queues and concurrency so overload becomes controlled delay or rejection rather than unbounded memory growth.
answer: Measure processing capacity and queue depth. For HTTP use bounded worker pools; for Kafka tune consumer concurrency and pause/resume or poll behavior.
mistakes: Using unbounded queues.
interview: Backpressure is a capacity boundary. Predictable throttling is safer than allowing memory and latency to grow indefinitely.

title: How do you design service-to-service timeout budgets?
short: Derive downstream deadlines from the top-level request budget rather than assigning the same timeout everywhere.
answer: A 1-second request cannot give three downstreams one second each. Propagate a deadline and reserve time for retries, serialization and response handling.
followups: What happens to async work after the request?
mistakes: Giving every dependency the full client timeout.
interview: Timeouts are budgets. I make every downstream respect the remaining deadline so work stops before the caller has already timed out.

title: How do you design an idempotent payment integration?
short: Use a durable payment intent and provider idempotency key, then reconcile ambiguous outcomes.
answer: A timeout can happen after the provider charges the card. Retrying with a new request risks double charge. Persist provider request IDs and query/webhook state to converge.
followups: How do you handle duplicate webhooks?
What if provider has no idempotency key?
mistakes: Creating a new payment after every timeout.
interview: The hardest case is an ambiguous timeout. I never create a second charge blindly; I retry the same logical operation or reconcile it.

title: How do you design graceful shutdown for microservices?
short: Drain traffic, stop accepting new work, finish safe in-flight work and stop consumers cleanly.
answer: Readiness should fail before termination, load balancers need time to drain, and consumers should stop polling and commit completed work. Long jobs need cancellation/recovery semantics.
code: readiness=false -> drain -> stop consumers -> close resources
followups: How do you handle long jobs?
mistakes: Only adding a shutdown hook.
interview: Graceful shutdown is an orchestration problem across the app, load balancer and worker system, not just a JVM hook.

title: How do you use distributed tracing across REST and Kafka?
short: Propagate standard trace context through HTTP and message headers and create spans at asynchronous boundaries.
answer: Inject trace context when producing, extract when consuming, and retain correlation metadata. Use sampling appropriate to volume.
code: traceparent header -> Kafka headers -> consumer span
followups: How do you sample high-volume topics?
mistakes: Starting a new unrelated trace for every message.
interview: I use standard trace propagation so a trace can show the request, producer, broker and consumer work rather than unrelated log IDs.

title: How do you read an execution plan for a slow query?
short: Find expensive operators, poor access paths and row-estimate errors, then compare actual behavior with the expected plan.
answer: Look for large scans, bad join strategies, repeated loops, sorts/spills and cardinality misestimation. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE where supported and verify indexes/statistics.
followups: When can a full scan be correct?
mistakes: Adding indexes without reading the plan.
interview: I identify the most expensive operator and validate why the optimizer chose it before changing indexes or SQL.

title: How do you choose composite index column order?
short: Match leading index columns to real equality, range and ordering predicates.
answer: Composite B-tree indexes are ordered by leading columns. A common pattern is equality predicates followed by range/order columns, but workload and plan evidence decide the final order.
mistakes: Always putting the highest-cardinality column first.
interview: I choose index order from query patterns, not a universal selectivity rule, then verify with the execution plan.

title: How do you prevent and recover from database deadlocks?
short: Use consistent lock ordering, short transactions and appropriate indexes; retry the whole transaction when a deadlock victim is detected.
answer: Different update orders create cycles. Consistent ordering and reduced transaction scope lower probability. Recovery must repeat the logical transaction because the database may have rolled it back.
code: UPDATE accounts SET ... WHERE id IN (?,?) ORDER BY id;
mistakes: Retrying only one SQL statement inside a rolled-back transaction.
interview: Deadlocks are a concurrency condition. I reduce them by design and make safe retries part of the application behavior.

title: When is keyset pagination better than OFFSET?
short: Keyset pagination scales better for deep pages because it seeks from the last seen key instead of skipping many rows.
answer: Use a deterministic composite ordering such as created_at plus id and query from the last tuple. It is ideal for feeds/infinite scroll but less convenient for arbitrary page numbers.
code: WHERE (created_at,id) < (?,?) ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC LIMIT 50
followups: How do you make ordering deterministic?
mistakes: Using a non-unique sort key alone.
interview: For large tables I prefer keyset pagination when users move sequentially through results.

title: How do you diagnose connection-pool exhaustion?
short: Inspect pool waiters, connection hold time, slow queries and database capacity before increasing pool size.
answer: A full pool can come from leaks, long transactions, slow queries or an undersized pool. Increasing it blindly can simply overload the database.
code: metrics: active, idle, pending, acquireLatency, usageDuration
followups: How do you choose pool size?
mistakes: Increasing max connections until the DB saturates.
interview: I correlate pool metrics with SQL and transaction traces to identify why connections are held too long.

title: How do window functions differ from GROUP BY?
short: GROUP BY collapses rows; window functions calculate across related rows while retaining row detail.
answer: Use ROW_NUMBER/RANK for ranking, LAG/LEAD for comparisons and SUM OVER for running totals.
code: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC)
mistakes: Using GROUP BY and losing row-level detail.
interview: I use GROUP BY for one row per group and window functions when I need group calculations alongside each original row.

title: How do you archive a huge table safely?
short: Move cold data in controlled batches or partitions and avoid giant delete transactions.
answer: Time-based partitioning can make retention a metadata operation. Otherwise archive by stable key in bounded batches while monitoring locks, WAL/redo and replication lag.
code: -- Prefer partition detach/drop for time-based retention.
mistakes: One huge DELETE during peak traffic.
interview: For very large historical data I prefer partition-based retention because dropping an old partition is safer than deleting millions of rows in one transaction.

title: How do you design an idempotent database command?
short: Use a unique business/idempotency key and atomic insert/update semantics.
answer: A unique constraint works across instances and restarts. Handle duplicate-key outcomes by returning or loading the existing logical result.
code: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_payment_key ON payments(idempotency_key);
followups: How do you return the original response?
How do you handle concurrent requests?
mistakes: Check-then-insert in separate non-atomic steps.
interview: Database uniqueness is a strong primitive for idempotency because the database arbitrates concurrent first attempts.

title: How do you perform a large data backfill safely?
short: Use small batches, stable keys, throttling and observability so the backfill does not starve production traffic.
answer: Prefer primary-key ranges, commit frequently, pause on replication lag or lock pressure, and make the job restartable.
code: UPDATE users SET new_col=... WHERE id > ? AND id <= ?;
mistakes: One massive transaction for millions of rows.
interview: A backfill is production workload. I make it resumable, bounded and adaptive to database health.

title: How do you diagnose lock contention?
short: Find blocked sessions, lock owners, transaction age and the SQL holding the resource.
answer: Long transactions and missing indexes often turn small updates into long lock waits. Correlate database lock views with application traces and transaction boundaries.
code: -- Inspect blocked/blocked-by sessions using DB-specific lock views.
mistakes: Only increasing timeout values.
interview: I identify who is waiting, who holds the lock and why the holder is slow. Then I shorten the transaction or improve the access path.

title: How would you design service-to-service authentication?
short: Authenticate workloads with short-lived identities and authorize the requested operation with least privilege.
answer: mTLS provides workload authentication at transport level; OAuth2 client credentials or signed service tokens provide application identity. Validate issuer, audience, expiry and scopes.
mistakes: Trusting any internal network caller.
interview: I separate workload authentication from authorization and avoid broad shared secrets. Every service validates identity and permissions at its boundary.

title: How do you secure JWT APIs beyond signature validation?
short: Validate issuer, audience, expiry, not-before and authorization claims, then enforce resource permissions.
answer: A valid signature proves origin, not that the token is intended for this API or action. Keep lifetimes short and rotate signing keys.
mistakes: Checking only signature and expiry.
interview: JWT validation is authentication; authorization still has to decide whether this caller may access this resource.

title: How do you design refresh-token rotation?
short: Rotate on every use and detect reuse to limit replay after token theft.
answer: Store a token family identifier and server-side state. A reused old token can indicate compromise, so revoke the family.
code: old -> refresh -> new; reuse old -> revoke family
followups: Where should refresh tokens be stored?
How do you revoke all sessions?
mistakes: Using one long-lived non-rotating refresh token.
interview: Rotation reduces the replay window and reuse detection gives a strong signal of token theft.

title: How do you defend a backend against SSRF?
short: Restrict outbound destinations and enforce network egress controls; do not allow arbitrary user URLs.
answer: Prefer allowlists, restrict protocols/ports, validate resolved addresses, handle redirects carefully and block access to internal/metadata ranges. Network policy is a second layer.
code: allowlistedHost -> outbound client; reject arbitrary schemes/addresses
followups: Why is IP blocking alone insufficient?
mistakes: Validating only the hostname string.
interview: SSRF defense must exist in both application validation and network egress policy because DNS and redirects can bypass naive URL checks.

title: How do you secure file uploads?
short: Validate size/content, generate server-side object names, isolate storage and authorize downloads independently.
answer: Do not trust extension or MIME type. Prevent path traversal, scan where required, and keep uploaded content outside executable web roots.
code:
UUID objectKey = UUID.randomUUID();
// store using server-generated key
followups: How do you handle zip bombs?
mistakes: Saving files using the original client filename.
interview: Uploads are untrusted data. I validate content and size, isolate storage and make access authorization explicit.

title: What is confused-deputy risk in microservices?
short: A service may use its own broad privileges to perform an action that the original caller was not allowed to perform.
answer: Keep service identities least-privileged and propagate user/delegation context when downstream authorization depends on the caller. Audit delegated actions.
code:
user -> service A -> privileged service B
// B must enforce intended caller permissions
mistakes: Giving every service admin credentials.
interview: Internal identity does not automatically mean unlimited authorization. I define the authorization boundary explicitly.

title: How do you rotate secrets without downtime?
short: Overlap old and new credentials during rollout, verify the new credential, then revoke the old one.
answer: Use a secret manager and versioned credentials. Consumers load the new version, establish successful connections, and only then should the old version be disabled.
code: old valid -> deploy new -> verify -> revoke old
followups: How do you rotate DB passwords with pools?
How do you detect stale instances?
mistakes: Revoking the old secret before all consumers switch.
interview: Secret rotation is a rollout problem. Overlapping validity avoids requiring a synchronized fleet restart.

title: How do you prevent cross-tenant authorization bugs?
short: Derive tenant identity from trusted authentication and enforce it at the data boundary.
answer: Never trust tenantId from the request as the authorization source. Include tenant predicates in data access and test horizontal access control explicitly.
code: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id=? AND tenant_id=?;
mistakes: Using client-supplied tenantId.
interview: Tenant isolation should survive a new endpoint being added incorrectly because the data boundary enforces it too.

title: How would you design Kubernetes autoscaling for a Java API?
short: Scale on demand/saturation signals while respecting startup time and downstream capacity.
answer: CPU may miss I/O saturation. Combine appropriate metrics, set min/max replicas, use readiness and graceful termination, and cap scale-out to protect the database.
followups: How do you prevent scale oscillation?
mistakes: Scaling only on CPU for an I/O-bound service.
interview: Autoscaling is a capacity loop. I choose signals tied to demand and verify that dependencies can absorb the additional load.

title: How do you design Kubernetes liveness/readiness correctly?
short: Readiness controls traffic; liveness detects unrecoverable process failure; startup probes protect slow initialization.
answer: A dependency outage should generally affect readiness rather than trigger liveness restarts. Probes should be cheap and representative of their purpose.
mistakes: Putting fragile downstream checks in liveness.
interview: I keep probe semantics separate so a transient database outage does not restart every pod and create a second incident.

title: How do you debug Kubernetes OOMKills for Java?
short: Compare container RSS with heap, metaspace, direct buffers, thread stacks and native memory.
answer: The container can be killed even when Java heap is below Xmx. Leave headroom for non-heap memory and inspect cgroup limits and GC behavior.
mistakes: Setting Xmx equal to the pod limit.
interview: I distinguish Java heap OOM from container OOMKill. The JVM and native libraries need memory outside the heap.

title: How do you design safe Kubernetes rolling releases?
short: Combine compatible application/database versions, readiness, graceful shutdown and controlled rollout parameters.
answer: Mixed versions must work together. Use readiness gates, termination grace periods, maxSurge/maxUnavailable and automated rollback signals.
mistakes: Incompatible schema changes during rolling deployment.
interview: A Kubernetes rollout is only safe if the application and schema are backward compatible during coexistence.

title: How do you design disaster recovery for a backend?
short: Define RPO/RTO first, then choose backups/replication and recovery procedures that meet them.
answer: Stateless services can be rebuilt from immutable artifacts; data requires tested backups or replication. Include DNS, secrets, dependencies and external providers in the recovery plan.
code:
RPO=5m; RTO=30m
// validate through restore drills
mistakes: Designing DR without RPO/RTO targets.
interview: I start with business recovery objectives and test restores/failover rather than assuming backups are usable.

title: How do you control noisy-neighbor behavior in cloud systems?
short: Enforce per-tenant quotas, concurrency limits and resource isolation.
answer: Measure resource consumption by tenant and apply rate/queue/database budgets. Premium tenants may require dedicated partitions or compute.
followups: How do you handle premium tenants?
mistakes: Using only a global rate limit.
interview: Noisy-neighbor protection is capacity fairness. I enforce limits at the earliest useful boundary and observe usage by tenant.

title: How do you optimize cloud cost without harming reliability?
short: Optimize cost per useful unit of work while preserving SLOs and resilience.
answer: Rightsize compute, autoscale, manage storage/log retention and data transfer, and use committed capacity for predictable workloads. Track cost per request/tenant alongside latency and availability.
followups: How do you control log spend?
mistakes: Cutting redundancy or observability without measuring risk.
interview: I optimize measured cost per unit of business work, not by blindly choosing the cheapest infrastructure.

title: Design a high-scale notification system
short: Separate request acceptance from asynchronous delivery across channel-specific workers.
answer: Persist a notification command, publish via an outbox, route to email/SMS/push workers, apply provider rate limits, retry transient failures and track delivery state idempotently.
followups: How do you prevent duplicate SMS?
How do you handle provider outage?
mistakes: Sending provider calls synchronously in the request thread.
interview: I would make acceptance durable and delivery asynchronous. Each channel has its own retry/rate policy and the overall state is an idempotent state machine.

title: Design a payment ledger
short: Use immutable double-entry entries and idempotent transaction identifiers.
answer: Every business transaction creates balanced debit/credit entries. Corrections are compensating entries. Derived balances can be optimized separately and reconciled.
code:
ledger(txId, accountId, debit, credit)
SUM(debit)=SUM(credit) per tx
followups: How do you reconcile external providers?
How do you handle concurrent writes?
mistakes: Overwriting a balance without an immutable ledger.
interview: For financial systems I prefer an append-only ledger because history remains auditable and balance invariants are explicit.

title: Design an inventory reservation service
short: Reserve stock atomically, expire abandoned reservations and make confirmation idempotent.
answer: Use an atomic conditional update or row lock so available stock cannot become negative. Reservations have expiry and order identity.
code: UPDATE inventory SET available=available-? WHERE sku=? AND available>=?;
followups: How do you handle hot SKUs?
mistakes: Read-then-update without protecting the invariant.
interview: The key invariant is never reserving more than available. I enforce it atomically in the database and model expiry as a recoverable state transition.

title: Design a distributed job scheduler
short: Persist jobs, claim them with leases and make execution idempotent.
answer: Workers claim ready jobs with owner/version/lease, heartbeat while working and allow expired leases to be retried. Exactly-once execution is usually not realistic, so handlers must tolerate duplicates.
code: UPDATE jobs SET owner=?, lease_until=? WHERE id=? AND lease_until < now();
followups: How do you scale millions of jobs?
How do you avoid duplicate execution?
mistakes: Assuming a lock provides exactly-once execution.
interview: I design for durable at-least-once execution with recovery. The job itself is responsible for idempotent side effects.

title: Design a large file upload service
short: Upload directly to object storage using scoped multipart/resumable URLs and keep metadata in a database.
answer: The backend creates an upload session and signed parts; the client transfers data directly. Completion records checksum/size and triggers asynchronous scanning/processing.
code:
POST /uploads -> signed parts
PUT -> object storage
POST /complete
mistakes: Proxying every large file through application servers.
interview: I keep large payloads out of the application cluster. The backend controls authorization and metadata while object storage handles transfer scale.

title: Design a high-throughput audit platform
short: Capture structured immutable audit events asynchronously and partition storage by useful access dimensions.
answer: Applications emit actor/action/resource/tenant/trace metadata. A durable broker buffers ingestion and consumers write searchable/retained projections.
followups: How do you search years of data?
mistakes: Treating ordinary application logs as a complete audit trail.
interview: Audit records are different from debug logs. I make them structured, access-controlled and durable, with retention and replay considerations.

title: Design a product catalog cache
short: Use cache-aside with bounded TTL and protection against hot-key stampedes.
answer: The database remains source of truth. Reads load on miss; writes invalidate or publish versions. Request coalescing and jittered expiry protect the database.
followups: How do you handle hot keys?
mistakes: Assuming cache invalidation is globally instantaneous.
interview: I define staleness tolerance first, then choose cache-aside and protect popular keys from synchronized expiry.

title: Design an e-commerce checkout system
short: Use explicit order state, idempotent commands and asynchronous coordination between inventory and payment.
answer: Create an order intent, reserve inventory, authorize payment and transition state. Outbox/events connect services; compensation handles failures.
followups: How do you prevent duplicate checkout?
mistakes: Trying to wrap every service in one distributed ACID transaction.
interview: I optimize checkout for correctness: durable state, idempotency and compensations rather than a distributed transaction.

title: Design a public API rate limiter
short: Use a distributed token bucket or sliding-window algorithm and expose predictable client behavior.
answer: Shared atomic state is required across instances. Return 429 with Retry-After and protect the limiter store with timeouts and a defined failure policy.
followups: How do you avoid hot keys?
mistakes: Using per-instance synchronized counters.
interview: I choose the algorithm from burst requirements, enforce it atomically across instances and decide explicitly what happens if the limiter store fails.

title: Design a distributed cache for a high-read backend
short: Use cache-aside, bounded memory and explicit invalidation/staleness semantics.
answer: Choose keys and TTLs, protect hot keys, measure hit rate and keep the source of truth authoritative. For critical correctness, use versioning or bypass cache when stale data is unsafe.
followups: How do you handle cache failure?
mistakes: Adding Redis without defining consistency or eviction.
interview: Caching is a consistency decision as much as a performance decision. I define acceptable staleness before selecting the strategy.
